Prepare for the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians with an online exam prep course built around organized study, electrical trade knowledge, code navigation, safety standards, and practice-oriented review. This course is designed for journeyman electrician candidates who want a structured way to study the subjects associated with electrical installation, maintenance, troubleshooting, repair, and code-compliant work.

The NASCLA Journeyman Electrician Exam - Online Exam Prep Course helps candidates work through a broad range of electrical topics without relying on random or disconnected study sessions. The course supports a focused preparation process that brings together National Electrical Code review, workplace safety, electrical theory, wiring methods, wiring protection, equipment requirements, fire alarm systems, plans, specifications, and troubleshooting concepts.

Because the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination is open book, successful preparation involves more than memorizing facts. Candidates need to understand the electrical principles behind each question, recognize which reference applies, locate relevant information efficiently, and interpret the complete requirement. An organized online course can help candidates build these skills through repeated exposure to trade-focused material and reference-based study.

The course is intended to be used alongside the listed examination references. Books are not identified as included with this online course. Candidates should obtain the required editions separately and confirm the current reference requirements before their scheduled examination.

The listed references include the 2023 National Electrical Code, federal OSHA construction and general industry regulations, NFPA 70E, Ugly’s Electrical References, NFPA 72, and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications. Together, these publications address code requirements, workplace safety, electrical hazards, formulas, calculations, fire alarm systems, and the theory used in practical electrical work.

Online preparation allows candidates to study in a more consistent and manageable format. Instead of attempting to read every publication from beginning to end without direction, students can organize their preparation by subject, reinforce important concepts, identify weaker knowledge areas, and practice using the references as working tools.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians is part of the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program. It is intended for individuals who have developed the knowledge and skills needed to perform electrical installation, maintenance, and repair work in accordance with applicable standards and codes.

The examination evaluates journeyman-level electrical knowledge across multiple trade areas. Preparation may involve interpreting electrical plans and specifications, applying basic electrical safety practices, solving theory questions, selecting testing procedures, troubleshooting electrical systems, and using code requirements for different types of installations.

National Electrical Code preparation is a major part of studying for a journeyman electrician examination. Candidates should understand how the NEC is organized and how to use its index, table of contents, articles, definitions, tables, exceptions, informational notes, and cross-references.

Code questions may involve branch circuits, feeders, services, grounding and bonding, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, boxes, raceways, cables, equipment, motors, transformers, special occupancies, special equipment, emergency systems, and communication systems. Candidates should learn how general requirements interact with rules that apply to a particular installation or piece of equipment.

Safety preparation may involve both OSHA regulations and NFPA 70E. Candidates should be able to distinguish between construction-industry requirements, general-industry requirements, and electrical safety-related work practices. Study areas may include hazard recognition, employee protection, personal protective equipment, safe work procedures, electrical shock hazards, arc-flash hazards, and workplace responsibilities.

Electrical theory remains essential even in an open-book exam. Candidates may need to work with voltage, current, resistance, power, series circuits, parallel circuits, alternating-current principles, transformers, motors, and common electrical formulas. Understanding why a formula applies is just as important as entering numbers into a calculator.

Plans and specifications may require candidates to interpret symbols, schedules, notes, circuit information, equipment locations, conductor information, and written project requirements. Troubleshooting topics may require the candidate to evaluate circuit behavior, identify likely faults, select testing equipment, and apply a logical diagnostic process.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for following the current examination rules governing permitted references, markings, tabs, calculators, identification, and testing procedures.

Open-book testing does not mean that every answer can be found quickly without preparation. Candidates must recognize the subject, choose the correct book, locate the applicable section, read the requirement carefully, and determine how it applies to the question. A candidate who is unfamiliar with the references may lose significant time searching through the wrong publication or section.

The online exam prep course supports a study method centered on understanding and navigation. Candidates can strengthen their ability to connect electrical questions with the appropriate code article, safety regulation, theory concept, table, formula, or fire alarm requirement.

Reference navigation should become part of regular study. Candidates should practice using the index and table of contents, locating major articles, reading definitions, identifying exceptions, checking table notes, and following cross-references. The goal is to build a repeatable process for finding and confirming information under timed conditions.

Each book serves a different purpose. The National Electrical Code addresses installation requirements. OSHA publications address federal workplace safety standards. NFPA 70E focuses on electrical safety-related work practices. NFPA 72 addresses fire alarm and signaling systems. Ugly’s Electrical References provides compact field information, while Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications supports the principles and calculations behind electrical work.

Candidates should review the current candidate information before test day. Examination policies may regulate highlighting, underlining, permanent tabs, loose papers, handwritten notes, removable tabs, inserts, and other modifications to reference materials.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination does not automatically issue a license. The examination may satisfy a trade-testing requirement for participating licensing agencies, but candidates must still meet the requirements of the state or local authority responsible for the desired credential.

  1. Choose the licensing jurisdiction. Identify the state, county, city, or regulatory agency where you intend to apply for a journeyman electrician license.
  2. Confirm examination acceptance. Verify that the agency accepts the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians for the classification you are pursuing.
  3. Review eligibility requirements. Determine whether the agency requires electrical work experience, apprenticeship completion, classroom education, employer verification, or other qualifications.
  4. Complete the applicable application. Submit the forms and supporting documents required by NASCLA or the administering licensing agency.
  5. Register and schedule the examination. Follow the current instructions for examination registration, payment, approval, and scheduling.
  6. Prepare with the correct references. Obtain the listed editions and use the online exam prep course to organize code, theory, safety, and trade review.
  7. Take the examination. Follow all testing rules concerning arrival, identification, calculators, reference materials, security, and prohibited items.
  8. Submit the examination result. Follow the applicable process for transmitting the passing result to an agency that accepts the NASCLA examination.
  9. Finish the licensing process. Complete any remaining experience, documentation, fee, background, insurance, or administrative requirements established by the licensing authority.

State Requirements

The NASCLA Accredited Examination Program is not a national electrician license. It provides an examination result that may be used in place of a state-specific trade examination by participating regulatory agencies.

Journeyman electrician requirements vary by jurisdiction. A licensing authority may require documented work experience, completion of an apprenticeship program, technical education, employer affidavits, examination approval, application fees, identification documents, or other supporting information.

Some states regulate journeyman electricians through a statewide licensing agency. Other locations may use county, city, or municipal licensing systems. The scope of work, supervision rules, renewal requirements, continuing education obligations, and license classifications may differ.

Candidates should confirm the requirements for the exact jurisdiction in which they intend to work. An agency may accept the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination while still requiring the applicant to complete additional state or local steps.

A passing examination result demonstrates that the candidate met the testing standard. The receiving licensing agency remains responsible for reviewing the full application and determining whether the applicant qualifies for a license.

Reference Books

    The 2023 National Electrical Code contains requirements for electrical installations, including wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, and communication systems.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1926 - OSHA Construction Industry Regulations
    This OSHA reference addresses federal workplace safety requirements for construction activities. It supports study involving construction hazards, electrical safety, personal protective equipment, employee protection, and safe work practices.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1910 - OSHA Occupational Safety and Health Standards
    This publication contains federal occupational safety and health standards for general industry. It supports preparation related to workplace conditions, electrical hazards, equipment, employee protection, and employer responsibilities.
  • NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    NFPA 70E addresses electrical safety-related work practices, including hazard assessment, shock protection, arc-flash protection, approach boundaries, personal protective equipment, and energized work considerations.
  • Ugly’s Electrical References, 2023
    Ugly’s Electrical References is a compact field resource containing electrical formulas, tables, conversions, conductor information, motor data, and practical reference material.

    NFPA 72 provides requirements for fire alarm systems, signaling systems, initiating devices, notification appliances, emergency communications, inspection, testing, and related system functions.

    This publication connects electrical theory with practical NEC applications. It supports study involving voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, formulas, calculations, and electrical problem-solving.

The books listed above are reference materials associated with the examination and course study. They are not stated as included with this online exam prep course. Candidates should obtain the required publications separately and use the editions specified for their examination.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive study plan should combine technical review, reference navigation, calculation practice, and timed problem-solving. Reading alone may not be enough to build the speed and judgment needed for an open-book electrical examination.

Begin by learning the organization of each publication. Identify the purpose of the book, the types of questions it can answer, and the fastest way to locate information. Practice selecting the appropriate reference before searching for the answer.

For NEC preparation, study definitions, branch circuits, feeders, services, conductors, overcurrent protection, grounding, bonding, wiring methods, equipment, motors, transformers, special occupancies, special equipment, emergency systems, and communication systems.

For theory preparation, work through electrical formulas and calculations. Review Ohm’s law, power, resistance, series circuits, parallel circuits, voltage relationships, current relationships, transformers, motors, and common trade calculations. Check units carefully and practice recognizing the information provided in each problem.

For safety preparation, compare OSHA construction standards, OSHA general industry standards, and NFPA 70E. Candidates should understand how the references differ and which publication applies to a particular workplace or electrical safety question.

Timed practice can help reveal whether a candidate is struggling with technical knowledge, book navigation, code interpretation, or calculation accuracy. When reviewing an incorrect answer, determine why it was missed and return to the applicable reference or concept.

A useful open-book process is to identify the subject, select the most likely reference, locate the section, read the complete requirement, review exceptions and notes, and then confirm the answer. Practicing this process repeatedly can improve efficiency and confidence.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps candidates approach the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician exam with organized study guidance and trade-focused review. The online exam prep course is structured to support electrical knowledge, code navigation, safety awareness, theory review, and practice-oriented preparation.

Instead of studying without a clear direction, candidates can work through electrical subjects in a more organized sequence. This helps connect individual rules and formulas with the broader responsibilities of a journeyman electrician.

The course supports preparation involving the National Electrical Code, OSHA regulations, NFPA electrical safety requirements, fire alarm standards, electrical calculations, plans, and troubleshooting concepts. Candidates can use the material alongside their reference books to strengthen both knowledge and navigation skills.

Reference navigation is especially important for an open-book test. 1 Exam Prep encourages candidates to learn how the books are organized, practice using indexes and tables, identify frequently used sections, and develop a consistent process for locating answers.

Practice-oriented preparation can also help candidates identify weaker topics before the examination. Reviewing missed questions and returning to the underlying code section or theory principle can turn an incorrect answer into a useful study opportunity.

The course is designed to build a more focused study routine and greater familiarity with journeyman-level electrical topics. It does not guarantee a passing examination result, license approval, or acceptance by a regulatory agency.

Prepare for the Virginia Concrete Contracting examination with an online exam prep course focused on the technical knowledge, reference-book navigation, and test-taking skills needed for the Concrete Contracting specialty. This Virginia Concrete Contractor exam prep course is designed for candidates working toward the Concrete Contracting specialty, commonly identified by the abbreviation CEM, through the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation Board for Contractors.

The Virginia Concrete Contracting specialty covers work associated with processing, proportioning, batching, mixing, conveying, and placing concrete using materials common to the concrete industry. The scope also includes concrete finishing, coloring, curing, repairing, testing, sawing, grinding, grouting, film barriers, sealing, waterproofing, construction and assembly of forms and molds, and the use of reinforcing steel.

Because the Virginia Concrete Contracting exam is open book, preparation requires more than memorizing construction facts. Candidates also need to understand where important information is located within the approved references and how to move efficiently between concrete standards, building-code requirements, OSHA regulations, excavation information, reinforcing-steel guidance, and formwork material. The goal of this course is to help organize those areas into a practical study process that supports both trade knowledge and reference navigation.

The examination covers estimating, layout and excavation, formwork, reinforcing steel, general concrete knowledge, and safety. These subjects reflect the everyday technical knowledge associated with concrete construction and require candidates to work comfortably with calculations, field practices, construction terminology, concrete materials, reinforcing methods, formwork principles, excavation procedures, and jobsite safety requirements.

An organized Virginia Concrete Contractor exam prep program can help you spend less study time searching randomly through large reference books and more time learning how the major exam topics connect. By becoming familiar with the books before test day, you can build a repeatable method for identifying keywords, locating relevant chapters and tables, and confirming answers efficiently during an open-book examination.

Exam Details

The Virginia Concrete Contracting examination is administered through PSI as part of Virginia's contractor specialty examination program. Candidates must receive the required eligibility approval before scheduling the specialty examination.

  • Examination: Virginia Concrete Contracting
  • Specialty Abbreviation: CEM
  • Testing Provider: PSI
  • Number of Questions: 50
  • Time Allowed: 120 minutes
  • Minimum Passing Score: 70%, or 35 correct answers
  • Exam Format: Computer-administered examination
  • Exam Type: Open book

The published examination content areas include:

  • Estimating: 5 items
  • Layout and Excavation: 10 items
  • Formwork: 6 items
  • Reinforcing Steel: 7 items
  • General Concrete: 16 items
  • Safety: 6 items

General Concrete represents the largest portion of the examination, but successful preparation should account for every content area. Layout, excavation, reinforcing steel, formwork, estimating, and safety collectively make up a substantial part of the test and should be included in a complete study plan.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Concrete Contracting examination is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing permitted reference materials because reference books are not supplied at the testing location.

Open book does not mean that every answer can be found quickly without preparation. The examination has 50 questions and a 120-minute time limit, giving candidates an average of approximately 2.4 minutes per question. Familiarity with the organization of the reference books can therefore be an important part of exam preparation.

PSI permits reference books to be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination, but the references must otherwise remain unmarked. Study guides are not permitted as exam-room references. Loose papers and unbound reference material are not permitted. References may be organized using permanent tabs, while removable tabs such as temporary flags are not allowed.

Before test day, spend time learning each book's table of contents, index, major chapters, common tables, definitions, and frequently referenced sections. When practicing questions, identify the wording that points toward a particular reference. For example, a question involving trench conditions may direct you toward excavation or OSHA material, while a question involving reinforcing-bar placement may require a reinforcing-steel reference.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation through the Board for Contractors. The Concrete Contracting specialty is one component of the contractor licensing process, and candidates should follow the requirements that apply to their intended license class and business structure.

  1. Determine the appropriate Virginia contractor license class and specialty. Applicants seeking to perform concrete contracting work should identify Concrete Contracting as the applicable specialty when appropriate for their business activities.
  2. Complete required pre-license education. Virginia requires eight hours of pre-license education for new contractor licenses. The course covers contractor business and regulatory requirements and is separate from trade-specific examination preparation.
  3. Identify the required Qualified Individual. Virginia contractor licenses must identify a Qualified Individual for each specialty listed on the license. The individual associated with the Concrete Contracting specialty must satisfy the applicable Board requirements.
  4. Obtain examination eligibility. The Board reviews eligibility requirements before a candidate takes the contractor specialty examination.
  5. Schedule and take the applicable examination through PSI. Once eligible, the candidate can schedule the Virginia Concrete Contracting examination through PSI.
  6. Complete the contractor license application process. After satisfying the applicable examination and licensing requirements, submit the required contractor application materials to the Virginia Board for Contractors.

Depending on the license class being pursued, additional business examination requirements may apply. Candidates should prepare for the examinations and licensing requirements associated with their specific Virginia contractor license application, not only the Concrete Contracting specialty examination.

State Requirements

The Virginia Board for Contractors regulates contractor licensing in the Commonwealth. Every licensed contractor must identify a Qualified Individual for each specialty on the license. Concrete Contracting is one of the specialties for which qualified individuals may be required to complete a Board-approved specialty examination.

Virginia also requires eight hours of pre-license education for new contractor licenses. For Class A and Class B applicants, the education must be completed by a member of responsible management or the designated employee. For Class C applicants, a member of responsible management must complete the pre-license education. This pre-license education requirement is separate from a trade exam prep course.

Candidates preparing for the Concrete Contracting exam should make sure their licensing application, Qualified Individual designation, education requirements, and required examinations are coordinated with the license class they intend to obtain. Passing a specialty examination is one part of the overall contractor licensing process and does not by itself issue a Virginia contractor license.

Studying directly from the reference materials helps candidates learn both the subject matter and the location of information they may need during the open-book test.

  • ACI 318-14: Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete and Commentary
    Contains widely used structural concrete requirements covering materials, design provisions, reinforcement, development and splicing, durability, construction requirements, and structural concrete practices.
  • Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, 17th Edition

  • Pipe and Excavation Contracting
    Covers excavation-related construction knowledge, including earthwork practices, trenching, equipment, site conditions, layout considerations, and work associated with underground construction.
  • SP-4 Formwork for Concrete, 2014, 8th Edition
    Provides detailed information on concrete formwork, including form materials, design considerations, wall and slab forms, shoring and bracing, construction loads, form pressures, safety considerations, and practical formwork methods.
  • Placing Reinforcing Bars
    Focuses on reinforcing-steel practices such as bar identification, placement, supports, ties, splices, detailing concepts, tolerances, and field procedures used when placing reinforcement in concrete construction.

A strong study strategy should combine trade knowledge with repeated reference-book practice. Start by separating the examination into its six published content areas: estimating, layout and excavation, formwork, reinforcing steel, general concrete, and safety. This makes a large collection of technical information easier to manage.

For estimating questions, review basic quantity calculations and the process of interpreting dimensions and project information. Formwork preparation should include form materials, pressures, supports, shoring, bracing, loads, and removal considerations. Reinforcing-steel study should focus on bar placement, supports, splices, identification, and common field practices.

General Concrete deserves substantial attention because it accounts for 16 of the 50 scored questions. Safety preparation should include the OSHA requirements relevant to concrete operations, excavation, equipment, fall hazards, protective systems, and general construction-site conditions.

When you answer a practice question, identify which book contains the supporting information and practice finding the relevant section. Repeating this process develops familiarity with the vocabulary used in both examination questions and the reference indexes.

During the actual examination, consider answering familiar trade-knowledge questions first and marking more time-consuming reference questions for review. Avoid spending too much of the examination searching for a single answer. With a 120-minute limit, effective time management and fast book navigation can be just as important as knowing the technical material.

Prepare for the Virginia Concrete Contractor licensing process and establish the business foundation needed to operate professionally with The 1 Package: All-Inclusive New Virginia Concrete Contractor Exam, Licensing & Business Setup Solution. This comprehensive package combines technical exam preparation, professionally highlighted and tabbed rental reference books, 1 year of course access, Application Service, Business Formation, EIN Filing with the IRS, and Contractor Compliance Guidance.

The package is designed for candidates pursuing Virginia's Concrete Contracting specialty (CEM). Concrete contracting involves much more than placing and finishing concrete. The Virginia specialty covers concrete processing, proportioning, batching, mixing, conveying, placement, finishing, curing, testing, repair, formwork, reinforcing steel, sealing, waterproofing, and other work within the defined scope of concrete construction.

Preparing for the CEM examination therefore requires knowledge across several connected construction subjects. Candidates should understand concrete materials and mixtures, structural concrete requirements, reinforcing steel, formwork, layout, excavation, estimating, and construction safety. The examination is open book, making familiarity with the technical references another important part of an organized preparation strategy.

The 1 Package combines those study resources with licensing and business setup support. Candidates receive an extended preparation period, assistance with the contractor application process, support establishing an LLC or Corporation, EIN Filing with the IRS, and Contractor Compliance Guidance. The result is a structured solution for candidates who want help moving from exam preparation toward establishing their Virginia concrete contracting business.

What You Get

  • Included Book: Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
  • Included Book: International Building Code, 2021
  • Included Book: ACI 318-14: Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete and Commentary
  • Included Book: Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, 17th Edition
  • Included Book: Pipe and Excavation Contracting
  • Included Book: Placing Reinforcing Bars
  • Included Book: SP-4 Formwork for Concrete, 2014, 8th Edition
  • Included Book: NASCLA Contractor’s Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Virginia 11th Edition
  • Included Book: Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code, 2021 Edition, USBC
  • Book Preparation: All included rental books are highlighted and tabbed for exam preparation.
  • Course Access: 1 year of course access.
  • Application Service: Included with this package.
  • Business Formation (LLC or Corporation): Assistance establishing the customer’s business entity so the contracting business is legally structured and prepared to operate professionally.
  • EIN Filing with the IRS: Assistance obtaining an Employer Identification Number for business functions such as opening business bank accounts, managing taxes, hiring employees, and conducting business operations professionally.
  • Contractor Compliance Guidance: Assistance understanding contractor compliance requirements relevant to establishing and operating a Virginia contracting business.
  • Package Cost: $2,810.
  • Refundable Book Deposit: $700.
  • Total Initial Cost: $3,510 — All-Inclusive, No Hidden Fees.
  • Rental Period: The $700 deposit is refundable when the rental books are returned in similar condition within 1 year.
  • Order Preparation: Please allow up to 15 business days for The 1 Package book orders.

Exam Details

The Virginia Concrete Contracting examination is the technical specialty examination associated with the CEM designation. Candidates pursuing this specialty must complete the applicable Virginia Board for Contractors qualification process before taking the specialty examination administered through PSI.

  • Exam Name: Concrete Contracting Examination
  • Specialty: Concrete Contracting (CEM)
  • Number of Questions: 50
  • Time Allowed: 120 minutes
  • Minimum Passing Score: 70%, or 35 correct answers
  • Exam Administrator: PSI

The examination evaluates knowledge across the primary technical areas involved in concrete contracting. The published content outline includes estimating, layout and excavation, formwork, reinforcing steel, general concrete, and construction safety.

  • Estimating: 5 questions
  • Layout and Excavation: 10 questions
  • Formwork: 6 questions
  • Reinforcing Steel: 7 questions
  • General Concrete: 16 questions
  • Safety: 6 questions

General Concrete is the largest examination area, while Layout and Excavation is the second largest. Candidates should still prepare across all six categories because formwork, reinforcement, safety, and estimating represent substantial portions of the technical examination.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Concrete Contracting examination is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing permitted reference materials because the testing center does not provide the books.

Virginia's examination information permits approved references to be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted. Removable tabs are not allowed, and written notes in the references are prohibited.

All rental references in The 1 Package are highlighted and tabbed for exam preparation. Candidates should use the books repeatedly during the study period so the location of major topics becomes familiar. Highlighting and tabs are most effective when combined with an understanding of the underlying technical material.

The 120-minute testing period provides an average of approximately two minutes and twenty-four seconds for each of the 50 questions. Efficient reference navigation can therefore be valuable. Candidates should practice identifying the subject first and then choosing the appropriate book before beginning a detailed search.

For example, reinforcing-steel questions may require Placing Reinforcing Bars or ACI 318. Formwork topics may point toward SP-4. Concrete materials and mixture questions can be researched in Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, while excavation questions may require Pipe and Excavation Contracting. Construction safety questions may require 29 CFR Part 1926.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation Board for Contractors. A contractor business must satisfy the requirements applicable to its license class and requested classification or specialty.

  1. Establish the business entity. The 1 Package includes Business Formation assistance for an LLC or Corporation.
  2. Obtain an EIN. EIN Filing with the IRS is included with the package.
  3. Determine the appropriate Virginia contractor license class. Virginia licenses contractors as Class A, Class B, or Class C.
  4. Select the Concrete Contracting specialty. Virginia identifies Concrete Contracting with the abbreviation CEM.
  5. Identify the Qualified Individual. The contractor business must designate a Qualified Individual who meets the applicable requirements for the specialty.
  6. Document qualifying experience. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the experience requirements applicable to the requested license class and specialty.
  7. Complete required pre-license education. New Virginia contractor applicants must satisfy the applicable eight-hour pre-license education requirement.
  8. Complete the required examination process. The Qualified Individual must receive the applicable approval and successfully complete the CEM examination.
  9. Prepare the contractor application. Application Service is included with The 1 Package.
  10. Address applicable contractor compliance requirements. Contractor Compliance Guidance is included with the package.

Successful completion of the CEM examination is one part of the licensing process. A Virginia contractor license is issued only after the applicant satisfies the applicable licensing requirements.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Concrete Contracting as work connected with processing, proportioning, batching, mixing, conveying, and placing concrete composed of materials common to the concrete industry.

The specialty also includes finishing, coloring, curing, repairing, testing, sawing, grinding, grouting, placement of film barriers, sealing, and waterproofing. Construction and assembly of forms, molds, slipforms, pans, centering, and the use of reinforcing steel are also included within the CEM scope.

Virginia regulations also recognize that the Commercial Building Contractor, Residential Building Contractor, and Highway/Heavy Contractor classifications provide authority for concrete work within their respective scopes.

Exam Details

The Virginia Farm Improvement Contracting examination is the technical specialty examination associated with the FIC designation under the Virginia Board for Contractors. PSI administers the specialty examination for Qualified Individuals.

  • Exam Name: Farm Improvement Contracting Examination
  • Specialty Abbreviation: FIC
  • Number of Questions: 40
  • Time Allowed: 90 minutes
  • Minimum Passing Score: 70%, or 28 correct answers
  • Exam Administrator: PSI

The published examination outline divides the test among several construction disciplines:

  • Excavating and Site Work: 5 questions
  • General Concrete: 6 questions
  • Masonry: 5 questions
  • Rough Carpentry and Metal Framing: 8 questions
  • Manufactured Trusses: 5 questions
  • Roofing and Siding: 6 questions
  • Safety: 5 questions

Rough Carpentry and Metal Framing is the largest individual examination category. General Concrete and Roofing and Siding also represent significant portions of the test. Candidates should nevertheless prepare for every subject because questions can move quickly between site work, concrete, masonry, framing, trusses, roofing, siding, and safety.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Farm Improvement Contracting examination is an open-book test. Candidates must bring their own permitted reference materials because testing centers do not provide the books.

Permitted references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted. Removable tabs and references containing written notes are not permitted under the published examination rules.

The included rental books are highlighted and permanently tabbed to support organized navigation. Candidates should still use the books regularly throughout their 1 year of course access so they become familiar with each reference and understand where important subjects are located.

The exam allows 90 minutes for 40 questions, providing an average of approximately two minutes and fifteen seconds per question. Efficient reference selection can help candidates preserve time for calculations, technical interpretation, and detailed code questions.

For example, excavation questions may point toward Pipe and Excavation Contracting. Concrete questions may require Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures. Masonry questions may lead to Modern Masonry, while framing questions may require Carpentry and Building Construction. Manufactured truss questions may require the BCSI reference, and safety questions may require 29 CFR Part 1926.

Passing the FIC technical examination is one part of the Virginia contractor licensing process. The business must also satisfy the applicable licensing requirements before the requested contractor license and specialty are issued.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Farm Improvement Contracting as the installation, repair, or improvement of a nonresidential farm building or structure, a nonresidential farm accessory-use structure, or additions to those structures.

The Virginia Commercial Building Contractor and Residential Building Contractor classifications also provide authority for Farm Improvement Contracting work within their respective scopes.

The FIC specialty does not provide authority for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or gas-fitting functions. Contractors performing separately regulated trade work must have the applicable authority for those services.

The contractor business must identify a Qualified Individual for the FIC specialty who meets the experience and technical examination requirements applicable to that designation. Virginia also requires the contractor business to satisfy the requirements associated with its selected Class A, Class B, or Class C license.

Virginia requires successful completion of the applicable examination before a contractor applies for licensure. The technical examination is therefore an important milestone, but it remains part of a broader licensing process involving the business entity, Qualified Individual, education, examinations, documentation, and contractor application.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong FIC preparation plan should follow the exam content outline. Rough Carpentry and Metal Framing deserves substantial attention because it is the largest individual section. Candidates should review layout, structural members, floor systems, wall framing, roof framing, connections, and general building practices.

Manufactured Trusses should be studied separately from conventional framing. Metal plate connected wood trusses involve specific handling, installation, restraint, and bracing procedures. The BCSI reference provides dedicated technical guidance for this area.

General Concrete preparation should cover concrete ingredients, mixture proportions, water-cement relationships, strength, durability, placement, consolidation, curing, and testing. Candidates should focus on understanding how concrete behaves under practical construction conditions.

Masonry study should include brick, block, stone, mortar, layout, tools, materials, and construction methods. Familiarity with the terminology in Modern Masonry can make both technical interpretation and reference navigation more efficient.

Excavating and Site Work requires knowledge of site preparation, grading, excavation methods, trenching, soil movement, and equipment. These subjects may also connect directly with construction safety requirements in 29 CFR Part 1926.

Roofing and Siding should include roof components, roofing systems, exterior coverings, siding, weather protection, and the relationship between structural framing and the building envelope.

Safety should remain part of the study schedule throughout preparation. Nonresidential farm-building construction can involve excavation, scaffolds, ladders, elevated work, framing, power tools, material handling, and equipment hazards.

Virginia contractor licenses are divided into Class A, Class B, and Class C. The class determines the monetary size of work the business may undertake.

Class A applies when a single contract or project is valued at $150,000 or more, or when the total value of construction undertaken during a 12-month period is $1 million or more.

Class B applies when a single contract or project is valued at $30,000 or more but less than $150,000, or when the total value of construction during a 12-month period is $250,000 or more but less than $1 million.

Class C applies to covered work valued at more than $1,000 but less than $30,000 for a single contract or project and within the applicable annual limitation established by Virginia law.

Exam Details

The Virginia Refrigeration Contracting examination is the technical specialty examination associated with the REF designation. Virginia requires a Qualified Individual for each classification or specialty on a contractor license, and REF is one of the specialties requiring pre-approval and successful completion of a Board-approved technical examination.

The Virginia Refrigeration Contracting examination contains 50 questions. Candidates receive 120 minutes to complete the exam and must achieve a minimum passing score of 70%, or 35 correct answers.

The examination content is divided into the following subject areas:

  • General Knowledge and Requirements: 16 questions
  • Refrigeration Piping: 10 questions
  • Refrigerants: 5 questions
  • Refrigeration Systems and Controls: 12 questions
  • Testing and Inspection: 7 questions

General Knowledge and Requirements represents the largest single category. Refrigeration Systems and Controls and Refrigeration Piping also account for a substantial portion of the examination. Candidates should devote appropriate study time to all five areas while giving additional attention to the higher-weighted subjects.

The examination may include questions based on the reference materials as well as general trade knowledge and accepted industry practices. Practical experience can be valuable, but candidates should also prepare for technical terminology, written code requirements, tables, system concepts, and questions that require efficient use of reference materials.

Virginia uses PSI as its examination vendor for Qualified Individual contractor specialty examinations. Successful completion of the required examination must occur before applying for contractor licensure for a designation that requires the technical exam.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Refrigeration Contracting examination is an open-book test. Candidates must bring their own permitted reference materials because references are not supplied at the testing site.

The examination is currently based on the 2021 edition of applicable ICC codes for code questions, including the International Mechanical Code. Candidates should therefore become familiar with the structure of the 2021 International Mechanical Code before examination day.

References may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted. Removable tabs such as temporary flags are not allowed. Reference materials containing handwriting are not permitted, and candidates may not write in their books during the examination session.

Open-book testing rewards preparation and efficient navigation. With 50 questions and 120 minutes, candidates have an average of approximately 2.4 minutes per question. Searching unfamiliar books for every answer can quickly consume testing time.

Some books included with The 1 Package are highlighted and tabbed for exam preparation. Candidates should use the one-year study period to learn what each tab identifies, understand how chapters are organized, and practice locating technical and code information without unnecessary searching.

The International Mechanical Code is used for applicable code requirements. Learning which reference is most likely to contain the needed information is an important open-book testing skill.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered through the Virginia Board for Contractors. Contractor licenses combine a license class with one or more classifications or specialties. The class determines the applicable level of contracting authority, while the classification or specialty determines the type of work the business may perform.

  1. Choose the appropriate contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select Refrigeration Contracting. Refrigeration Contracting is identified by the REF specialty abbreviation.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. Every contractor business must identify a Qualified Individual for each classification or specialty requested.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirement. The Qualified Individual must document sufficient experience for the selected contractor class.
  5. Complete the REF examination approval process. Refrigeration Contracting requires pre-approval and successful completion of the applicable technical examination.
  6. Prepare for and pass the specialty examination. Technical study should include refrigeration knowledge, reference navigation, and 2021 International Mechanical Code material.
  7. Complete contractor pre-license education. Virginia requires eight hours of Board-approved pre-license education for new contractor licenses.
  8. Complete applicable business examinations. Class A and Class B businesses must identify a Designated Employee who satisfies the applicable business examination requirements.
  9. Establish the business entity. The 1 Package includes Business Formation assistance for an LLC or Corporation.
  10. Obtain the EIN. EIN Filing with the IRS is included with this package.
  11. Complete and submit the contractor application. Application Service is included to support the licensing application portion of the process.

The technical specialty examination is only one part of Virginia contractor licensing. The contractor business must also satisfy requirements involving the appropriate class, Qualified Individual, Responsible Management, pre-license education, applicable Designated Employee examinations, and completed application.

State Requirements

Virginia requires licensed contractor firms to identify a Qualified Individual for every classification or specialty printed on the license. The Qualified Individual must have the appropriate amount of experience and must satisfy examination requirements when an examination is required for that designation.

For a Class C contractor, the Qualified Individual must have at least one year of experience in the applicable classification or specialty. A Class B Qualified Individual must have at least three years of experience, and a Class A Qualified Individual must have at least five years of experience.

The Qualified Individual must also have the required relationship to the contractor business. Virginia requires the individual to be a full-time employee or a member of Responsible Management as provided by the contractor licensing requirements.

REF is specifically identified as a designation requiring pre-approval and successful completion of the applicable examination. An Experience Verification Form is required as part of the qualification process for designations that require a technical examination.

Virginia also requires eight hours of Board-approved pre-license education for every new Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor license. For Class A and Class B applicants, the requirement is completed by a member of Responsible Management or the Designated Employee. For Class C applicants, a member of Responsible Management completes the course.

The pre-license course is a basic business course addressing regulations, statutes, and requirements relevant to contractor businesses. It is separate from the REF technical examination and separate from the Class A and Class B contractor business examinations.

Open-book testing makes reference familiarity an essential part of preparation. Having several large books available is useful only when candidates understand how to navigate them. Candidates should know which reference is most appropriate for a particular subject and be comfortable using indexes, tables of contents, chapters, technical tables, and code sections.

Permitted references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination according to applicable testing rules. Permanent indexing methods can help candidates move between important sections efficiently. Some books included with The 1 Package are highlighted and tabbed for exam preparation, giving students an organized starting point for reference practice.

A question involving a specific residential code requirement may lead to the International Residential Code. A question involving practical construction or framing methods may be easier to address through Carpentry and Building Construction or the Builders Technical Supplement. Contractor business questions can require a different reference entirely.

With 160 minutes available for 80 questions, candidates have an average of approximately two minutes per question. Effective preparation therefore combines construction knowledge with selective reference use rather than attempting to search multiple books for every answer.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing combines a license class with one or more classifications or specialties. A company pursuing Residential Building Contracting must satisfy the requirements associated with both the selected contractor class and the RBC classification.

  1. Determine the appropriate contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select Residential Building Contracting. The applicable classification abbreviation is RBC.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. The contractor business must identify a Qualified Individual for the RBC classification.
  4. Document the required experience. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the applicable experience requirement associated with the contractor class.
  5. Complete the RBC examination process. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the applicable technical examination requirement.
  6. Complete contractor pre-license education. New Virginia contractor license applicants must complete eight hours of Board-approved pre-license education.
  7. Complete applicable Class A or Class B business examinations. A Designated Employee must satisfy the applicable business examination requirements for these classes.
  8. Establish the business entity. The 1 Package includes Business Formation assistance for an LLC or Corporation.
  9. Obtain an EIN. EIN Filing with the IRS is included with this package.
  10. Complete the contractor application. Application Service is included to support the application portion of the licensing process.

The technical examination is only one piece of the complete process. The contractor business must also address its license class, Responsible Management, Qualified Individual, Designated Employee when applicable, pre-license education, business structure, and application requirements.

State Requirements

Virginia requires a Qualified Individual for every classification or specialty listed on a contractor license. The Qualified Individual must have relevant work experience within the scope of the classification being requested.

Current Virginia contractor requirements establish a minimum of one year of applicable experience for a Class C Qualified Individual, three years for Class B, and five years for Class A. The Qualified Individual must also meet the required relationship to the contractor business.

Residential Building is one of the classifications requiring the applicable examination process. Experience verification is part of the qualification process for designations that require examination approval.

Virginia also requires eight hours of Board-approved pre-license education for all new Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses. This pre-license course is a general contractor business course and is separate from the RBC technical examination.

Class A and Class B applicants must also address separate Designated Employee business examination requirements. These business examinations cover contractor management and Virginia-specific subjects and should be treated as a separate study track from the technical Residential Building examination.

The RBC classification focuses on residential construction within Virginia's defined scope. It does not independently authorize separately regulated electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or gas-fitting services. A contractor offering those services must have the applicable authority for that work.

Applicants must be at least 18 years old and meet an approved combination of practical trade experience and formal vocational training. Current qualification pathways include:

  • 3 years of practical experience plus 120 hours of formal vocational training.

Applicants using a vocational-training pathway must provide documentation of their formal training, while practical experience must be verified according to Virginia's application requirements.

Exam Details

The Virginia Tile, Marble, Ceramic and Terrazzo Contractor examination is the Qualified Individual technical examination associated with the TMC specialty. A Virginia contractor business requesting this specialty must identify a Qualified Individual who meets the applicable experience requirements and successfully completes the required examination.

The TMC examination contains 50 questions. Candidates receive 120 minutes to complete the test and must achieve at least 70%, or 35 correct answers, to meet the passing requirement.

Major areas of preparation include:

  • Plan Reading and Estimating
  • General Tile Knowledge
  • Grouting and Finishing
  • Adhesives
  • Tile Installation
  • Terrazzo
  • Safety

General Tile Knowledge and Tile Installation are central parts of preparation. Candidates should understand tile types, substrates, surface preparation, setting materials, layout, movement accommodation, installation methods, curing, joints, and accepted industry practices.

Terrazzo requires separate attention because it involves specialized materials, systems, specifications, installation procedures, and finishing techniques. Candidates whose daily work primarily involves ceramic, porcelain, stone, or glass tile should not overlook this portion of the specialty.

Plan Reading and Estimating also require preparation involving dimensions, areas, quantities, layouts, project plans, and specifications. Grouting, adhesives, finishing, and OSHA construction safety are additional subjects that contribute to overall examination performance.

Virginia contractor licenses combine a license class with one or more classifications or specialties. Tile, Marble, Ceramic and Terrazzo Contracting is identified by the specialty abbreviation TMC.

  1. Determine the contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select the TMC specialty. The business requests Tile, Marble, Ceramic and Terrazzo Contracting as the applicable specialty.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. The contractor business must designate the individual who qualifies the company for TMC work.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirement. The Qualified Individual must document experience appropriate to the requested contractor class and specialty.
  5. Submit experience verification. TMC requires pre-approval for the technical examination.

The Virginia Board for Contractors licenses contractor businesses and requires a Qualified Individual for each applicable classification or specialty designation.

The Qualified Individual must be a full-time employee of the business working at least 30 hours per week or a member of Responsible Management. Current minimum experience requirements are 1 year for Class C, 3 years for Class B, and 5 years for Class A.

An Experience Verification Form is required when a Qualified Individual requests a specialty that requires pre-approval for a technical examination. TMC is included among the specialties requiring that examination process.

Moving up to a Virginia Journeyman Electrician license is a milestone—because it represents more than hands-on skill. The exam reflects that responsibility. It’s not just “what you know,” but how quickly and correctly you can apply it under time pressure.

This Virginia 2023 Journeyman Electrician Exam Prep and Study Guide is built around what helps most on open-book licensing exams: practice. You’ll work through 12 practice exams plus 2 full final exams designed to help you develop a steady test-day process—read with precision, recognize what the question is truly testing, confirm the right rule in your reference, and choose the best answer without second-guessing.

Practice exams do more than measure readiness—they build it. Each set helps you:

  • Improve speed by reducing “search time” in your reference books
  • Increase accuracy by reinforcing correct code interpretation and common exam patterns
  • Strengthen confidence by training under realistic, question-after-question conditions
  • Spot weak areas early so you can study what matters instead of rereading everything

Whether you’re coming straight from journeyman work or returning to testing after time away, this study guide gives you a structured routine you can follow: practice, review, correct, repeat—until the exam format feels familiar and manageable.

Exam Details

Virginia tradesman licensing is regulated by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation (DPOR) through the Board for Contractors. The tradesman examinations are administered by PSI. PSI’s Virginia Individual License and Certification Candidate Information Bulletin lists the Journeyman Electrician portion as:

  • 90 items
  • 270 minutes to complete
  • Passing score: 63
  • Exam fee: $100 (fee is valid for one year from the date of payment; non-refundable and non-transferable)

The bulletin also provides a topic breakdown that includes both professional standards and technical electrical knowledge. Journeyman-level candidates should be ready for questions that cover ethics and professional responsibility (standards of practice, standards of conduct, renewal and reinstatement, definitions, qualification for licensure, revocation of licensure) as well as broad electrical competencies (services, feeders, branch circuits, grounding and bonding, conductors and cables, raceways and boxes, motors and controls, utilization equipment, lighting, and more).

Because the exam includes both rule-based and application-based questions, your study plan should train two skills at the same time: (1) recognizing what the question is really asking, and (2) confirming the correct rule quickly in your references.

Open Book Test

Virginia tradesman examinations are open book. PSI’s bulletin states that all examinations are open book and that you must bring your own references because they are not provided at the test site.

Open-book rules that matter on exam day:

  • No study guides are permitted.
  • No loose papers or unbound references are permitted.
  • If a reference is downloaded from the internet, it must be spiral bound or hole-punched and placed in a binder, or stapled in the left-hand corner.
  • References may be highlighted, underlined, and/or indexed prior to the exam.
  • Reference materials containing any writing are not allowed into the examination.
  • You may not write in reference materials during the exam session.
  • References may be tabbed with permanent tabs only; no removable tabs are allowed.

Open book doesn’t remove the pressure—it shifts it. The test rewards the electrician who can find and apply the correct requirement efficiently. That’s why timed practice is so effective: it forces you to develop a reliable method for locating answers, confirming exceptions, and moving forward without losing momentum.

Licensing Steps

Virginia’s Board for Contractors oversees the licensing process for individual tradesmen. The general pathway to a Virginia Journeyman Electrician license includes meeting eligibility requirements, applying for examination approval, completing the PSI exam, and maintaining your license through renewal.

  1. Confirm you meet journeyman eligibility. Virginia regulations list experience standards used for examination approval (see State Requirements below).
  2. Prepare documentation. DPOR requires applicants to submit documentation of identification, vocational training, and experience.
  3. Submit your application to the Board. The Board approves applications for testing, and PSI notes a notification is sent after your application is approved.
  4. Register and schedule through PSI. Once approved, you pay and schedule your exam through PSI’s registration process.
  5. Take and pass the Journeyman Electrician exam. Use an open-book strategy with strong reference navigation and time management.
  6. Renew on time. Electrician licenses in Virginia expire on a three-year cycle and have continuing education requirements tied to renewal.

This study guide is designed to support the “exam performance” part of that journey—helping you practice the same type of thinking you’ll need on test day, not just review concepts in the abstract.

State Requirements

Virginia’s DPOR Tradesman Exam & License Application lists multiple journeyman qualification pathways. For journeyman applicants, the application instructs candidates to select one option that matches their experience and training history. The listed routes include (among others):

  • Four years of practical experience in the trade and 240 hours of formal vocational training in the trade.
  • Five years of practical experience and 160 hours of formal vocational training.
  • Six years of practical experience and 80 hours of formal vocational training.
  • Seven or more years of practical experience and 40 hours of formal vocational training.
  • Associate’s degree or certificate of completion from at least a two-year program in a tradesman-related field from an accredited community college or technical school, plus two years of practical experience in the trade.
  • Bachelor’s degree or certificate of completion in an engineering curriculum related to the trade, plus one year of practical experience in the trade.
  • Eight years of practical experience in the trade (verified by individuals who have observed the applicant’s work in the trade).
  • Individuals currently certified or licensed as a journeyman or master outside Virginia (with the required Letter of Good Standing and proof of licensure).

Because Virginia offers multiple routes, your best prep plan is one that focuses on what remains consistent across all applicants: NEC understanding, strong navigation habits, careful reading, and steady pacing. That’s what this combo is built to support.

With 270 minutes to complete the Journeyman Electrician portion, many candidates assume time won’t be an issue. But long exams create a different challenge: staying consistent deep into the testing session. Your preparation should build both technical readiness and test stamina.

Use the 12 practice exams to train the skills the exam actually demands:

  • Question recognition: learn to spot whether you’re being tested on definitions, general electrical knowledge, installation requirements, grounding and bonding rules, conductor sizing concepts, raceways/boxes, motors/controls, or professional standards.
  • Reference navigation: practice locating the correct chapter, section, or topic efficiently. The goal is to confirm answers without turning every question into an extended search.
  • Answer discipline: reduce careless mistakes by reading the question carefully, noting qualifiers (like “most appropriate,” “required,” “minimum,” or “best”), and confirming what is actually being asked.
  • Pacing and momentum: learn when to confirm in the reference and when to move on, so you don’t sacrifice easy points for one time-consuming question.

A practical way to study with this guide:

  • Start with one timed practice exam. Use it as a baseline to identify what topics cost you the most points.
  • Review missed questions with purpose. Don’t stop at the correct answer—identify why your choice was wrong and what rule or concept you needed to apply.
  • Create a “repeat list.” Any topic you miss twice becomes a priority until it turns into a strength.
  • Save the 2 full final exams for the end. Treat them like dress rehearsals: timed, distraction-free, and as close to exam conditions as possible.

Open-book exams reward a calm, methodical approach. When you’ve practiced enough, you stop “hoping you’ll find it” and start knowing exactly how you’ll handle each question type.

  • Step 3: Review by proving the answer. Don’t just memorize the correct choice. Locate the supporting NEC section (or regulation reference) and confirm why it applies. This trains the open-book skill that matters most: accurate confirmation under time pressure.
  • Step 4: Train “two-pass pacing.” First pass: answer questions you can solve efficiently and keep moving. Second pass: return to tougher questions with the time you protected. This prevents one hard question from stealing time from ten easier ones.
  • Step 5: Use the 2 full final exams as simulations. Save them for late in your prep. Take them timed, in a quiet setting, with minimal interruptions. Review carefully afterward—your biggest improvements often happen after a full simulation because it reveals pacing and endurance issues you can still fix.

Practice exams also help you eliminate the “small leaks” that cost big points: choosing an answer without reading an exception, grabbing a table value without checking notes, confusing similar NEC rules, or rushing through a question that hinges on one key phrase. The more you practice, the less those patterns show up.

  • Reference materials containing any writing are not allowed into the examination.

Licensing Steps

  4. Receive approval to test. PSI’s bulletin states the Board approves applications for testing and that notification is sent upon approval.
  5. Schedule your exam with PSI. Once approved, you register and schedule through PSI using the exam scheduling process.
  6. Pass the Master Electrician exam. Use an open-book strategy that includes reference navigation, time management, and careful reading—then complete the exam within the allotted time.
  7. Renew on time and complete required continuing education. Virginia regulations outline the license expiration timeframe and continuing education requirements tied to renewal and reinstatement.

Virginia defines “master” in a trade as a person who can plan and lay out installation details and supervise the work, using sufficient working knowledge to comply with the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. That definition aligns with the Master Electrician scope: it’s not just doing the work—it’s directing it and ensuring compliance.

General requirements for licensure or certification in Virginia regulations include items such as:

  • Being at least 18 years of age
  • Submitting documentation of identification, vocational training, and experience
  • Following Board and testing organization rules for examination conduct (failure to comply can be grounds for denial)

Master eligibility standards (experience): Virginia regulations state that an applicant for examination to be licensed as a master in a trade must meet one of the following experience standards:

  • Held a valid journeyman license in the trade for a minimum of one year; or
  • Nine years of practical experience in the trade; or
  • Held a valid residential HVAC tradesman or residential plumber tradesman license in the trade for which licensure is desired for three years (this pathway applies to those specific residential trade licenses).

License term, renewal, and continuing education: Virginia regulations state that licenses issued to electricians expire three years from the last day of the month in which they were issued (as shown on the license). As a condition of renewal or reinstatement, individuals holding tradesman licenses with the trade designation of electrical must satisfactorily complete three hours of continuing education for each designation, and that continuing education must be from a provider approved by the Board.

Fees (selected items from Virginia regulations and PSI):

  • Original tradesman license by examination: $150.00 (Virginia regulations)
  • Tradesman renewal fee: $160.00 (Virginia regulations)
  • Master Electrician exam fee: $125 (PSI bulletin)

  • Step 3: Build a “repeat list.” Any topic you miss twice becomes a priority until it turns into a strength.
  • Step 4: Final rehearsal. Save the two full finals for late-stage prep. Take them under realistic conditions to confirm pacing and readiness.

Open-book strategy tip: Your references help most when you use them with intention. Instead of flipping randomly, practice using a consistent approach: identify the keyword, locate the likely chapter/section, confirm the rule, then move on. Over time, you’ll speed up naturally—and that’s where exam confidence comes from.

Virginia's Class A and Class B contractor business examinations are administered for the Board for Contractors through PSI. The Designated Employee of a Class A or Class B contractor business must meet the applicable business examination requirements.

Class B requires two examination portions:

  • Virginia Portion
  • General Portion

Class A requires three examination portions:

  • Virginia Portion
  • General Portion
  • Advanced Portion

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licenses are issued to business entities and sole proprietors rather than to the Designated Employee personally. Class A and Class B applicants must satisfy several business, personnel, education, financial, and examination requirements.

  1. Determine the appropriate license class. Decide whether the business requires a Class A or Class B contractor license based on the contract and annual project-value limits established by Virginia law.
  2. Select the appropriate classification or specialty. The license class determines project-size limits, while the classification or specialty determines what type of contracting work the business may perform.
  3. Identify the Designated Employee. Class A and Class B businesses must name a Designated Employee who is at least 18 years old and is either a full-time employee of the business or a member of responsible management.
  4. Complete the required Pre-License Education. A Designated Employee or member of responsible management for a new contractor business must complete an approved eight-hour business course. This is a separate licensing requirement from the Class A/B examination.
  5. Complete the appropriate business examination. Class B requires the Virginia and General portions. Class A requires the Virginia, General, and Advanced portions.
  6. Name a Qualified Individual. The business must have a Qualified Individual for each classification or specialty requested. The Qualified Individual must meet the applicable experience and prerequisite requirements.
  7. Meet the financial requirement. Class A and Class B firms must provide the required financial verification or satisfy the applicable surety-bond alternative.
  8. Submit the contractor license application. Complete the DPOR Board for Contractors application and provide the documentation required for the business, Designated Employee, Qualified Individual, and requested classification or specialty.

The eight-hour Virginia contractor Pre-License Education requirement is separate from this exam prep course. 1 Exam Prep also offers the Virginia 8 Hour Pre-License Education Online Course for Contractors.

Virginia currently defines Class A contractors as contractors performing or managing construction, removal, repair, or improvements when a single contract or project is valued at $150,000 or more, or when the total value of applicable work performed within a 12-month period is $1 million or more.

Virginia currently defines Class B contractors as contractors performing or managing construction, removal, repair, or improvements when a single contract or project is valued at $30,000 or more but less than $150,000, or when the total value of applicable work performed within a 12-month period is $250,000 or more but less than $1 million.

For Class A, the Qualified Individual generally must have a minimum of five years of experience in the classification or specialty for which that person is qualifying. For Class B, the Qualified Individual generally must have a minimum of three years of experience.

Class A firms must verify net worth or equity of $45,000 through an accepted financial statement process, or may use the Board's permitted surety-bond alternative. Class B firms must verify net worth or equity of $15,000 or more, or may use the permitted surety-bond alternative.

The Designated Employee and Qualified Individual serve different functions. The Designated Employee fulfills the business examination requirement for a Class A or B firm. The Qualified Individual establishes qualification for the particular classification or specialty of work the business wants to perform. One person may satisfy multiple roles when that person meets all applicable requirements.

Virginia also requires a Board-approved eight-hour business course for new contractor license applicants. For Class A and Class B firms, the course must be completed by the Designated Employee or a member of responsible management. The eight-hour Pre-License Education requirement is separate from the Class A/B business examination.

What are the current Virginia Class A contract limits?

Class A applies when a single contract or project is $150,000 or more or the applicable total construction work performed within a 12-month period is $1 million or more.

The Designated Employee satisfies the applicable Class A or Class B business examination requirement. The Qualified Individual demonstrates the experience and prerequisites required for the classification or specialty in which the contractor business seeks to be licensed.

Virginia uses PSI to administer the Class A and Class B contractor business examinations for the Board for Contractors.

Preparing for a technical contractor examination requires more than memorizing definitions.
