Exam Details

The Virginia Commercial Building Technical Contractor examination is administered through PSI as part of the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation Board for Contractors examination program.

The CBC technical examination contains 80 questions. Candidates have 180 minutes to complete the examination and must achieve a minimum passing score of 70%, or 56 correct answers.

The examination content is divided into ten major subject areas:

  • Site Work – 8 questions
  • Concrete including Reinforcement – 9 questions
  • Masonry – 9 questions
  • Metals – 9 questions
  • Carpentry – 9 questions
  • Thermal and Moisture Protection – 8 questions
  • Associated Trades and Finishes – 7 questions
  • Safety – 7 questions
  • Estimating and Plan Reading – 8 questions
  • General Building Code Requirements – 6 questions

The Associated Trades and Finishes category includes subjects such as drywall, metal stud framing, insulation and moisture control, doors, windows, and glazing. General Building Code Requirements include life safety and egress, accessibility, fire protection requirements, and general code provisions.

Concrete, masonry, metals, and carpentry are among the largest individual sections, with 9 questions each. Site Work, Thermal and Moisture Protection, and Estimating and Plan Reading each contain 8 questions, making balanced preparation across the entire content outline important.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Commercial Building Technical Contractor examination is an open book test. Candidates may bring approved reference materials into the examination center subject to PSI's reference-material rules.

Approved references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted. Removable tabs and temporary flags are not allowed. Reference materials containing written notes are not permitted, and candidates may not write in their references during the examination.

Open-book testing does not eliminate the need to study. The examination covers a large number of technical subjects, and searching through unfamiliar references can consume valuable testing time. Candidates should practice connecting each subject area with the appropriate reference before exam day.

A question involving occupancy, means of egress, fire protection, or other building-code requirements may lead to the International Building Code 2021. Accessibility questions may require familiarity with Accessible and Usable Buildings and Facilities, while construction safety questions should direct candidates toward 29 CFR Part 1926.

Concrete questions may involve The Contractor's Guide to Quality Concrete Construction, while reinforcing-steel questions may direct attention toward Placing Reinforcing Bars. Questions involving masonry can point toward Modern Masonry, and metals questions may require the steel joist technical digest or the SDI Manual of Construction with Steel Deck.

Practice identifying the subject first, selecting the appropriate reference second, and locating the information third. This method can help make open-book exam preparation more efficient.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Board for Contractors within the Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation. Contractor licenses include a license class and one or more classifications or specialties that determine the work the business is authorized to perform.

  1. Determine the appropriate Virginia contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select the Commercial Building Contractor classification. Virginia identifies this classification with the abbreviation CBC.
  3. Designate the Qualified Individual. The business must identify a Qualified Individual for the classification requested.
  4. Meet applicable experience requirements. The Qualified Individual must document the experience required for the applicable contractor license class.
  5. Complete required pre-license education. New Virginia contractor applicants must satisfy the applicable Board-approved pre-license education requirement.
  6. Complete applicable business examination requirements. Class A and Class B applicants must satisfy the business examination requirements associated with the Designated Employee.
  7. Receive approval for the CBC technical examination. CBC is a classification requiring pre-approval and successful completion of a technical examination.
  8. Prepare for the technical exam. Study the examination content areas and practice using the approved technical references.
  9. Schedule and take the examination through PSI. Follow the current PSI registration process after receiving eligibility.
  10. Complete the licensing application process. Passing the examination is one component of obtaining the Virginia contractor license and CBC classification.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Commercial Building Contractors as contractors whose work includes construction, remodeling, repair, improvement, removal, or demolition involving real property owned, controlled, or leased by another person for commercial, industrial, institutional, governmental, and accessory-use buildings or structures.

The Commercial Building Contractor classification is abbreviated CBC. The classification includes a broad range of construction functions associated with qualifying commercial, institutional, governmental, and accessory-use buildings and structures, including applicable multi-family housing.

The CBC classification does not provide authorization for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or gas-fitting services. Contractors performing those activities must hold the classifications or specialty authority required for that work.

The classification also does not authorize construction, repair, or improvement of dwellings and townhouses as defined under the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code.

Virginia requires applicants seeking the CBC classification to identify a Qualified Individual and satisfy applicable experience and examination requirements. The Commercial Building classification is among the Virginia classifications requiring pre-approval and successful completion of a technical examination.

Passing the technical CBC examination does not by itself issue a Virginia contractor license. The contractor business must also satisfy the requirements applicable to its license class, business structure, Qualified Individual, Designated Employee when applicable, pre-license education, application, and other Board requirements.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive study plan for the Virginia CBC examination should follow the official content outline and devote time to every major category. Because several subjects carry similar question counts, candidates should avoid concentrating exclusively on one trade.

For Site Work, study excavation, grading, trenching, earthwork, site preparation, and equipment-related concepts. Pipe and Excavation Contracting provides a focused reference for these topics.

For Concrete including Reinforcement, review concrete materials, preparation, placing, finishing, curing, reinforcement, and bar-placement practices. Use The Contractor's Guide to Quality Concrete Construction with Placing Reinforcing Bars to connect concrete work with reinforcement requirements.

The Masonry section requires familiarity with brick, block, stone, mortar, layout, tools, and common construction methods. Modern Masonry supports review of these trade subjects.

For Metals, candidates should become comfortable with steel joists, joist girders, steel decking, handling, erection, fastening, and related construction practices. Both the steel joist technical digest and the SDI steel deck manual are important references for this subject area.

Carpentry preparation should include framing, structural components, floor systems, walls, roofs, materials, layout, and construction terminology. Understanding practical construction processes can also make plan-reading and estimating questions easier to interpret.

Thermal and Moisture Protection includes roofing and building-envelope considerations. Candidates should review roofing systems, materials, installation methods, moisture protection, and related construction concepts.

For Associated Trades and Finishes, review drywall, metal stud framing, insulation and moisture control, doors, windows, and glazing. The Gypsum Construction Handbook is particularly useful for gypsum wall and ceiling systems.

Safety preparation should include repeated navigation of 29 CFR Part 1926. Candidates should know how to locate regulations involving common construction hazards rather than attempting to memorize the entire reference.

Estimating and Plan Reading requires practical construction knowledge combined with careful interpretation of dimensions, drawings, quantities, and project information. Practice reading questions carefully and keeping units consistent when calculations are required.

For General Building Code Requirements, become familiar with the organization of the International Building Code 2021 and the accessibility reference. Review life safety, means of egress, accessibility, fire protection, and general code provisions.

Timed reference practice is especially useful. Read a practice question, identify its subject, choose the likely reference, locate the appropriate section, and confirm the answer. Repeating this sequence helps build both technical knowledge and open-book navigation skills.

Exam Details

The Virginia Commercial Building Technical Contractor examination is administered through PSI as part of the Virginia Board for Contractors examination program. The technical examination is associated with the Commercial Building Contractor classification, abbreviated CBC.

The CBC technical examination contains 80 scored questions. Candidates must achieve a minimum passing score of 70%, or 56 correct answers. The total examination time is 180 minutes.

The examination content is divided into the following subject areas:

  • Site Work – 8 questions
  • Concrete including Reinforcement – 9 questions
  • Masonry – 9 questions
  • Metals – 9 questions
  • Carpentry – 9 questions
  • Thermal and Moisture Protection – 8 questions
  • Associated Trades and Finishes – 7 questions
  • Safety – 7 questions
  • Estimating and Plan Reading – 8 questions
  • General Building Code Requirements – 6 questions

Associated trades and finishes include areas such as drywall, metal stud framing, insulation and moisture control, doors, windows, and glazing. General building code requirements include subjects involving life safety and egress, accessibility, fire protection requirements, and general code provisions.

Concrete, masonry, metals, and carpentry each account for 9 questions, making these among the largest individual technical categories. Site Work, Thermal and Moisture Protection, and Estimating and Plan Reading each contain 8 questions and should also receive significant attention during preparation.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Commercial Building Technical Contractor examination is an open book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing their permitted reference materials because books are not supplied at the testing site.

Approved references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the exam. Permanent tabs may be used to organize permitted reference materials. Reference materials containing written notes are not permitted, and candidates may not write in the references during the examination.

The highlighted and tabbed format of this package is designed for candidates who want their technical references organized before beginning intensive exam practice. Highlighted sections can draw attention to important information, while permanent tabs can provide quicker access to frequently used chapters and subjects.

Effective open-book preparation requires more than simply knowing that an answer exists somewhere in a reference. Candidates should practice identifying the topic of a question and immediately connecting it with the most appropriate book.

A building code question may lead to the International Building Code 2021. Accessibility questions may require Accessible and Usable Buildings and Facilities. Concrete and reinforcement questions may involve Placing Reinforcing Bars or The Contractor's Guide to Quality Concrete Construction. Masonry questions can point toward Modern Masonry, while safety questions should lead candidates toward 29 CFR Part 1926.

With 180 minutes available for the examination, candidates should develop a study routine that combines construction knowledge with efficient reference lookup. Repeated practice using the highlighted and tabbed books can help make navigation more familiar before exam day.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation Board for Contractors. Contractor licenses are issued to business entities, and each license includes a class together with the classification or specialty that determines the type of work the contractor is authorized to perform.

  1. Determine the appropriate contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select the Commercial Building Contractor classification. Virginia identifies Commercial Building Contractor with the abbreviation CBC.
  3. Designate the appropriate Qualified Individual. The Qualified Individual demonstrates the technical qualification associated with the requested classification.
  4. Meet applicable experience requirements. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the experience requirements applicable to the license class and classification.
  5. Complete required pre-license education. Virginia requires eight hours of approved pre-license education for new Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  6. Complete the required examination process. Successful completion of required examinations occurs before applying for contractor licensure.
  7. Prepare for the CBC technical examination. Study the construction subject areas and become familiar with the technical reference books used for the exam.
  8. Practice open-book navigation. Use the highlighted sections, permanent tabs, indexes, tables of contents, and code organization to develop efficient lookup skills.
  9. Schedule the examination through PSI. Follow the applicable Virginia contractor examination registration and scheduling procedures.
  10. Complete the contractor license application requirements. The business must satisfy the applicable Virginia Board for Contractors requirements for the license class and CBC classification being requested.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Commercial Building Contractors as contractors whose contracts include construction, remodeling, repair, improvement, removal, or demolition on real property owned, controlled, or leased by another person involving commercial, industrial, institutional, governmental, and accessory-use buildings or structures.

The Commercial Building Contractor classification uses the abbreviation CBC. The classification includes a broad range of construction functions performed on qualifying commercial, institutional, governmental, and accessory-use buildings and structures, including multi-family housing where applicable under Virginia's contractor regulations.

The CBC classification does not provide authorization for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or gas-fitting services. Those activities require the appropriate classifications or specialties.

The CBC classification also does not authorize construction, repair, or improvement of dwellings and townhouses as those structures are defined by the applicable Virginia building code requirements.

Because the CBC classification encompasses significant commercial construction responsibilities, the technical examination covers multiple trades and construction disciplines. Candidates should be prepared to demonstrate knowledge of structural components, building materials, site operations, safety, building codes, accessibility, estimating, plans, and construction methods.

Preparation for the Virginia CBC technical exam should reflect the broad range of subjects on the examination. A useful strategy is to divide study time according to the exam categories and work directly with the reference most closely associated with each subject.

For Site Work, review excavation, grading, earthwork, trenching, and related site operations. Pipe and Excavation Contracting can help reinforce terminology, construction methods, and practical considerations associated with these activities.

Exam Details

The ICC Commercial Electrical Inspector E2 exam is an 80-question multiple-choice exam with a 3.5-hour time limit. The exam is based on commercial electrical inspection job tasks and requires candidates to use the National Electrical Code to determine whether electrical installations comply with applicable code requirements.

The exam content includes General Requirements, Conductors, Services, Branch Circuit and Feeder Requirements, Wiring Methods and Distribution Systems, General Use Equipment, Special Occupancies, Special Equipment, and Special Systems. These categories reflect the practical work of a commercial electrical inspector. Candidates should be prepared to inspect electrical installations for correct materials, proper ratings, required clearances, suitable wiring methods, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, equipment installation, and special system requirements.

General Requirements include plan reading, code terminology, communication, general code compliance, approved plans, specifications, materials, listing, labeling, and basic inspection procedures. Students should understand how to review the information available on the job site and how to communicate code requirements using the correct electrical terminology.

Conductors include conductor use, installation, type, insulation, markings, ampacity, splices, connections, terminals, and identification. Students should be ready to verify that conductors are properly selected and installed for the conditions described in the question.

Services are a major part of the ICC E2 exam. This area includes service size, service rating, service installation, service equipment, service conductor ampacity, working clearances, location, materials, grounding electrode conductors, grounding electrodes, bonding, and service-related installation requirements. Commercial electrical inspectors must be able to determine whether service installations meet code requirements and whether grounding and bonding provisions are properly applied.

Branch Circuit and Feeder Requirements include branch circuit installation, feeder installation, load calculations, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, equipment grounding conductors, ratings, materials, devices, and related commercial installation requirements. Students should be comfortable using the NEC to evaluate branch circuits and feeders for conductor size, load, equipment grounding, overcurrent protection, and installation conditions.

Wiring Methods and Distribution Systems include required outlets, boxes, enclosures, conduit bodies, panelboards, switchboards, raceways, cables, bus ducts, flexible cords, and fixture wires. Students should study the rules that control where wiring methods may be used, how they must be supported, how boxes and enclosures are sized, and how distribution equipment must be installed.

General Use Equipment includes switches, receptacles, luminaires, appliances, heating equipment, cooling equipment, motors, controllers, transformers, generators, capacitors, resistors, batteries, and miscellaneous electrical equipment. Candidates should be prepared to inspect equipment for proper type, use, rating, location, disconnecting means, protection, and installation.

Special Occupancies include hazardous locations, health care facilities, commercial garages, gas stations, bulk stations, and other occupancy-specific electrical installations. These questions often require careful reading because special occupancy rules may modify or add to general wiring requirements. Students should be prepared to identify when a special rule applies and which installation method or material is required.

Special Equipment and Special Systems include swimming pools, spas, fountains, electric signs, data equipment, emergency systems, legally required standby systems, optional standby systems, signaling systems, fire alarm systems, communications systems, CATV, fiber optics, and low-voltage circuits. These topics require students to understand equipment-specific and system-specific code provisions and how they affect commercial inspections.

Open Book Test

The ICC E2 Commercial Electrical Inspector exam is an open-book exam. The primary reference for this product is the 2020 National Electrical Code. Students should prepare carefully because open book does not mean the answers will be easy to find without practice. The 3.5-hour time limit requires candidates to locate information quickly, read NEC language accurately, and apply the correct article, table, exception, or definition to the question being asked.

A strong open-book strategy begins with knowing the layout of the 2020 NEC. Students should become familiar with Article 90, definitions, wiring and protection rules, wiring methods and materials, equipment for general use, special occupancies, special equipment, and special conditions. Students should also practice using the index, tables, article structure, fine print notes where applicable, and cross-references so they can move through the code efficiently during the exam.

Commercial electrical inspection questions often require exact reading. A question may ask for a minimum conductor ampacity, a required working clearance, a grounding or bonding requirement, a raceway support rule, an outlet requirement, an overcurrent protection condition, a hazardous location provision, or a fire alarm system requirement. Students should avoid answering from field memory alone. The correct answer must be based on the approved reference used for the exam.

When ready, candidates register for the proper ICC E2 exam through the applicable ICC testing process. The license has two major components: the class of license and the classification or specialty. Commercial Improvement Contracting is a specialty designation identified by the abbreviation CIC.

  1. Determine the appropriate contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses. The class determines the level of contracting activity permitted under Virginia's licensing structure.
  2. Select Commercial Improvement Contracting. Candidates pursuing commercial repair and improvement work within the CIC scope identify Commercial Improvement Contracting as the requested specialty.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. Each classification or specialty requires a Qualified Individual who meets Virginia's applicable criteria.
  4. Meet the experience requirement. The Qualified Individual must demonstrate the required amount of experience associated with the license class being requested.
  5. Complete the examination approval process. Commercial Improvement Contracting is one of the Virginia specialties requiring examination pre-approval and an Experience Verification Form for the Qualified Individual.
  6. Pass the CIC technical examination. Successful completion of the approved Commercial Improvement Contracting examination is required for the applicable Qualified Individual.
  7. Complete pre-license education. Virginia requires eight hours of approved pre-license education for new Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor license applicants.
  8. Complete any Class A or Class B business requirements. Class A and Class B businesses have additional Designated Employee and business examination requirements separate from the CIC trade examination.
  9. Submit the contractor license application. The business submits the required licensing information and supporting documentation to the Virginia Board for Contractors.

State Requirements

The Virginia Board for Contractors regulates contractor businesses engaged in construction, repair, removal, or improvement work on property owned by others. Contractor licenses consist of a license class and the classification or specialty that establishes the type of work the contractor may perform.

Each contractor business must identify a Qualified Individual for every classification or specialty requested. The Qualified Individual must be either a full-time employee of the business or a member of Responsible Management and must satisfy the applicable experience and qualification requirements.

Virginia's current contractor application identifies minimum Qualified Individual experience requirements of at least one year for Class C, three years for Class B, and five years for Class A. Commercial Improvement Contracting requires pre-approval for the specialty examination, and an Experience Verification Form must be submitted for the Qualified Individual seeking CIC qualification.

Virginia also requires eight hours of pre-license education for all new Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor applicants. For Class A and Class B applicants, the education must be completed by a member of Responsible Management or the Designated Employee. For Class C applicants, a member of Responsible Management completes the requirement.

Class A and Class B businesses have business examination requirements in addition to specialty qualification. This product is a Commercial Improvement Contracting book package focused on the CIC technical trade examination references.

Reference Books

  • Included Book: Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    A federal construction safety reference covering OSHA standards for the construction industry. It supports preparation for safety topics involving worker protection, construction hazards, equipment, fall protection, scaffolds, excavations, personal protective equipment, and other jobsite safety requirements.
  • Included Book: Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code, 2018
    A Virginia-specific code reference containing statewide building requirements. This reference helps candidates become familiar with Virginia construction code provisions and the organization of the Uniform Statewide Building Code.
  • Included Book: International Building Code, 2021
    A major commercial building code reference addressing construction requirements, building systems, occupancy, fire-resistance, means of egress, materials, structural provisions, and numerous other code subjects relevant to commercial construction.
  • Included Book: International Residential Code for One- and Two-Family Dwellings, 2021
    A comprehensive code reference addressing building requirements for one- and two-family dwellings, including structural components, materials, framing, exterior systems, and other construction provisions.
  • Included Book: Carpentry and Building Construction, 2016
    A practical construction reference covering carpentry, framing, building materials, construction methods, tools, structural components, and related trade knowledge. It is particularly useful for preparation involving rough carpentry and framing concepts.
  • Included Book: Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, 17th Edition
    A technical concrete reference addressing concrete materials, mixture design, properties, production, placement, curing, durability, and quality considerations. The CIC exam includes a dedicated concrete content area.
  • Included Book: Modern Masonry - Brick, Block, Stone, Clois E. Kicklighter, 10th Edition
    A masonry reference covering brick, block, stone, mortar, masonry tools, materials, layout, construction methods, and related trade practices. Masonry represents one of the larger subject areas on the CIC examination.
  • Included Book: Gypsum Construction Handbook, 7th Edition
    A technical reference covering gypsum products, drywall construction, wall and ceiling systems, assemblies, materials, installation practices, and related construction details useful for the drywall portion of CIC preparation.

Test Information and Study Materials

Effective CIC exam preparation should combine construction knowledge with frequent book-navigation practice. Because the examination includes several technical disciplines, begin by learning which reference is most useful for each major content area.

For safety questions, become comfortable using 29 CFR Part 1926. For concrete questions, practice finding information in Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures. Masonry questions should lead naturally to Modern Masonry, while drywall subjects may require the Gypsum Construction Handbook. Rough carpentry and framing topics may involve Carpentry and Building Construction or applicable code requirements.

Code navigation deserves its own study time. Learn how definitions, chapters, sections, exceptions, tables, and indexes are organized. A code question may require more than finding a keyword; candidates may need to understand how a general rule, exception, or table applies to a specific situation.

Practice under timed conditions. With 120 minutes for 50 questions, the average available time is limited. During practice sessions, identify the likely reference before opening a book. Then use tabs, indexes, and highlighted sections to locate the information and confirm the answer.

It is also useful to prioritize larger content areas without ignoring smaller ones. Rough carpentry and metal framing, masonry, concrete, and roofing and exterior siding account for a substantial portion of the published exam outline. Windows and doors, drywall, general code requirements, and safety remain important and should be included in a complete study schedule.

  3. Identify a Qualified Individual. The contracting business must designate an individual who meets the applicable qualification requirements for the CIC specialty.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirement. The Qualified Individual must document the amount of trade experience required for the class of contractor license being requested.
  5. Complete the required technical examination. Commercial Improvement Contracting is among the Virginia specialties that require the Qualified Individual to successfully complete a Board-approved technical examination.
  6. Complete Pre-License Education. New Virginia contractor businesses must satisfy the eight-hour Board-approved Pre-License Education requirement.
  7. Complete Class A/B Business requirements when applicable. Class A and Class B contractor businesses also require a Designated Employee who meets the applicable business examination requirements.
  8. Submit the contractor license application. Complete the required Board for Contractors application and submit applicable business, experience, examination, and supporting information.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Commercial Improvement Contracting as the service of providing repair or improvement work to structures that are not defined as dwellings and townhouses in the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code.

The Commercial Building Contractor classification also provides authority for commercial improvement work. However, the CIC specialty is narrower than the CBC classification and focuses specifically on repair and improvement rather than new commercial building construction.

The CIC specialty does not authorize construction of new buildings or accessory buildings. It also does not independently authorize electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or gas work.

Commercial Improvement Contracting includes the following specialties within its authorized scope:

  • Masonry Contracting
  • Painting and Wallcovering Contracting
  • Roofing Contracting

These specialties do not need to be listed separately on the contractor license when the business holds the CIC specialty and the work falls within its authorized scope.

The Qualified Individual must satisfy the applicable experience requirements for the contractor license class. Virginia generally requires two years of experience for a Class C Qualified Individual, three years for Class B, and five years for Class A.

New contractor applicants must also complete eight hours of Board-approved Pre-License Education. Prepare for the Virginia Drywall Contracting examination with organized online exam prep focused on the technical subjects, trade knowledge, and reference-navigation skills associated with the Virginia Drywall Contracting specialty (DRY). The Virginia Drywall Contracting - Online Exam Prep is designed for candidates who want a structured way to study drywall installation, gypsum systems, estimating, plan reading, taping, special applications, construction safety, and applicable building-code requirements.

Virginia defines Drywall Contracting as work involving the installation, taping, and finishing of drywall, panels and assemblies of gypsum wallboard, sheathing, and cementitious board. The specialty also includes installation of sheet-metal studs used for framing ceilings and nonstructural partitions.

The Virginia DRY examination is broader than a basic drywall-finishing test. Candidates should understand gypsum products, wall and ceiling assemblies, metal-stud framing, installation procedures, fasteners, joint treatment, specialized applications, estimating, plan interpretation, building-code requirements, and jobsite safety.

The reference materials associated with the examination include Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA), the Gypsum Construction Handbook, 7th Edition, the International Building Code, 2021, and the International Residential Code for One- and Two-Family Dwellings, 2021. Effective May 1, 2025, PSI bases applicable ICC code questions for this examination on the 2021 editions.

Because the Virginia Drywall Contracting examination is open book, online preparation should include more than memorizing trade terminology. Candidates benefit from understanding the technical concepts and learning how to locate supporting information efficiently in the reference books. A strong preparation routine combines subject review, practice-oriented questions, calculations, code navigation, and repeated reference use.

Exam Details

The Virginia Drywall Contracting examination is a technical specialty examination associated with the Virginia Board for Contractors. PSI administers the examination for candidates pursuing the DRY specialty.

  • Exam Name: Drywall Contracting Examination
  • Specialty Abbreviation: DRY
  • Number of Questions: 40
  • Time Allowed: 90 minutes
  • Minimum Passing Score: 70%, or 28 correct answers
  • Exam Administrator: PSI

The published examination outline divides the 40 questions into five major subject areas:

  • Estimating and Plan Reading: 6 questions
  • Materials and Installation: 18 questions
  • Taping: 4 questions
  • Special Applications: 6 questions
  • Safety: 6 questions

Materials and Installation is the largest section, accounting for 18 of the 40 questions. Candidates should devote substantial study time to gypsum products, panels, framing systems, installation methods, fasteners, walls, ceilings, sheathing, and other construction practices associated with drywall work.

Estimating and Plan Reading, Special Applications, and Safety each account for six questions, making them significant parts of the examination. Taping accounts for four questions and should include preparation involving joint treatment, compounds, tape, finishing procedures, and related drywall terminology.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Drywall Contracting examination is an open-book test. Candidates must bring their own permitted reference materials because the books are not supplied at the testing center.

PSI permits approved references to be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted. Removable tabs are not allowed. References containing written notes are not permitted, and candidates may not write in their reference materials during the examination.

With 90 minutes available for 40 questions, candidates have an average of approximately two minutes and fifteen seconds per question. Efficient reference navigation is therefore an important part of preparation. Candidates should practice deciding which reference applies before beginning a detailed search.

A question involving gypsum panels, metal framing, finishing, or wall and ceiling systems may point toward the Gypsum Construction Handbook. Commercial building-code questions may require the International Building Code, 2021. Residential code questions may require the International Residential Code, 2021, while workplace safety questions may require 29 CFR Part 1926.

A useful open-book strategy is to identify the subject, select the appropriate reference, locate the applicable section using the index or table of contents, and then evaluate the question using the technical information found there.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation Board for Contractors. Contractor businesses operate under a license class together with one or more classifications or specialty designations.

  1. Determine the appropriate Virginia contractor license class. Virginia contractor licenses are issued as Class A, Class B, or Class C.
  2. Select the Drywall Contracting specialty. Virginia identifies this specialty with the abbreviation DRY.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. The contractor business must provide a Qualified Individual for the specialty.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirement. Virginia requires minimum qualifying experience based on the selected contractor license class.
  5. Complete the applicable experience verification. Drywall Contracting is one of the specialties requiring a technical examination approved by the Board.
  6. Complete required pre-license education. New Virginia contractor license applicants must satisfy the state's eight-hour pre-license education requirement.
  7. Complete the required technical examination. The Qualified Individual must successfully complete the DRY examination.
  8. Complete any additional examination requirements associated with the selected contractor license class.
  9. Complete and submit the Virginia contractor license application and supporting documentation.

Passing the Drywall Contracting examination is one component of the Virginia contractor licensing process. Successful completion of the technical examination does not by itself issue a contractor license.

State Requirements

Virginia's current contractor regulations define Drywall Contracting as work involving the installation, taping, and finishing of drywall, panels and assemblies of gypsum wallboard, sheathing, and cementitious board, along with installation of sheet-metal studs for framing ceilings and nonstructural partitions.

The contractor business must identify a Qualified Individual for each classification or specialty designation. The Qualified Individual must meet Virginia's applicable employment, experience, examination, and qualification requirements.

Virginia currently identifies the minimum experience requirement for a Qualified Individual based on the contractor license class:

  • Class C: Minimum of 1 year of qualifying experience
  • Class B: Minimum of 3 years of qualifying experience
  • Class A: Minimum of 5 years of qualifying experience

The Virginia Board for Contractors requires a technical examination for Qualified Individuals seeking the DRY specialty. Contractor applicants must also satisfy any applicable business, education, examination, and application requirements associated with their requested license class.

  • International Residential Code for One- and Two-Family Dwellings, 2021

A productive Virginia DRY study plan should follow the examination content distribution. Materials and Installation represents almost half of the exam, so candidates should spend substantial time reviewing gypsum products, panel types, framing systems, ceilings, partitions, fasteners, installation methods, sheathing, and cementitious board.

Estimating and Plan Reading requires both construction knowledge and calculation practice. Special Applications can involve construction conditions that differ from standard wallboard installation. Study specialized gypsum assemblies, fire-related conditions, moisture considerations, code requirements, and other applications covered by the technical references.

Safety represents six questions and should remain part of the study plan from beginning to end. Drywall work often involves ladders, scaffolds, overhead installation, lifting and handling panels, powered tools, and other construction hazards. Candidates should become familiar with how the OSHA reference is organized and practice locating applicable requirements.

Code navigation should also be practiced deliberately. Since PSI now bases applicable ICC questions on the 2021 editions, candidates should use the 2021 IBC and 2021 IRC during preparation. Learn how the chapters are organized and practice recognizing whether a question involves commercial building requirements or residential construction requirements.

A strong online preparation routine combines trade review with reference practice. After studying a topic, answer practice-oriented questions and then locate the supporting information in the appropriate reference. This approach reinforces both technical understanding and open-book navigation.

When a question is answered incorrectly, review the reason for the mistake. Was the construction concept misunderstood? Was the wrong code book selected? Was an important word in the question overlooked? Was too much time spent looking in the wrong section? Identifying the cause helps make future study more productive.

Timed practice is useful as the examination approaches. Work toward maintaining a steady pace without rushing every question. Some questions may be answered directly from trade knowledge, while others require careful reference work or calculations.

The objective of preparation is not to memorize every page of four technical books. It is to build enough subject familiarity that candidates can understand the question, recognize the correct reference, locate detailed information when necessary, and work through the examination efficiently.

The Virginia DRY examination contains 40 questions.

Candidates have 90 minutes to complete the Virginia Drywall Contracting examination.

Because agricultural buildings can incorporate many different construction systems, candidates preparing for the FIC examination need broader technical knowledge than they would for a narrowly focused specialty.

The examination references include Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA), International Building Code, 2021, International Residential Code for One- and Two-Family Dwellings, 2021, Carpentry and Building Construction, 2016, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures, 17th Edition, Modern Masonry - Brick, Block, Stone, 10th Edition, Pipe and Excavation Contracting, and the BCSI: Guide to Good Practice for Handling, Installing, Restraining, and Bracing of Metal Plate Connected Wood Trusses, 2025.

Exam Details

The Virginia Farm Improvement Contracting examination is the technical specialty examination associated with the FIC designation under the Virginia Board for Contractors. The examination is administered by PSI.

  • Exam Name: Farm Improvement Contracting Examination
  • Specialty Abbreviation: FIC
  • Number of Questions: 40
  • Time Allowed: 90 minutes
  • Minimum Passing Score: 70%, or 28 correct answers
  • Exam Administrator: PSI

The published examination content is divided among seven technical areas:

  • Excavating and Site Work: 5 questions
  • General Concrete: 6 questions
  • Masonry: 5 questions
  • Rough Carpentry and Metal Framing: 8 questions
  • Manufactured Trusses: 5 questions
  • Roofing and Siding: 6 questions
  • Safety: 5 questions

Rough Carpentry and Metal Framing is the largest individual exam category, accounting for eight questions. General Concrete and Roofing and Siding each account for six questions. Excavating and Site Work, Masonry, Manufactured Trusses, and Safety each contribute five questions.

This distribution makes balanced preparation important. Candidates should be ready to move from a question about site excavation to one involving concrete, masonry, framing, truss bracing, roofing, or construction safety. Understanding how these subjects connect within a complete building project can make exam questions easier to interpret.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Farm Improvement Contracting examination is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing their own permitted reference materials to the examination because the books are not provided at the testing center.

Approved reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted. Removable tabs are not allowed, and references containing written notes are prohibited under the testing rules.

Open-book status does not mean every answer can be found quickly without preparation. Candidates have 90 minutes to answer 40 questions, providing an average of approximately two minutes and fifteen seconds per question. Spending several minutes searching an unfamiliar reference can create unnecessary time pressure later in the examination.

A useful strategy is to classify the question before reaching for a book. Excavation and site-work questions may lead to Pipe and Excavation Contracting. Concrete questions may require Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures. Masonry questions may point toward Modern Masonry, while framing questions may require Carpentry and Building Construction.

Questions involving metal plate connected wood trusses may require the BCSI reference. Safety questions may point toward 29 CFR Part 1926. Code-related questions may require the 2021 International Building Code or 2021 International Residential Code.

The goal is to build a repeatable process: identify the subject, choose the appropriate reference, locate the relevant section using the index or table of contents, and then evaluate the answer choices using the technical information found there.

Licensing Steps

  1. Determine the appropriate contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select the Farm Improvement Contracting specialty. Virginia identifies this specialty with the abbreviation FIC.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. The contractor business must designate an individual who meets the applicable requirements for the specialty.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirements. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the experience requirements associated with the selected license class and specialty.
  5. Complete required pre-license education. New Virginia contractor applicants must complete the applicable eight-hour approved pre-license education requirement.
  6. Complete the required FIC technical examination.
  7. Complete any additional examinations associated with the selected contractor license class.
  8. Prepare the contractor license application and supporting documentation.
  9. Submit the required materials through the Virginia Board for Contractors licensing process.

Passing the Farm Improvement Contracting examination is one component of Virginia contractor licensing. Successful completion of the technical examination does not by itself issue a contractor license.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Farm Improvement Contracting as the service that provides for the installation, repair, or improvement of a nonresidential farm building or structure, a nonresidential farm accessory-use structure, or additions to those buildings or structures.

The Commercial Building Contractor and Residential Building Contractor classifications also provide authority for Farm Improvement Contracting work within their applicable scopes.

The FIC specialty does not provide authority for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or gas-fitting functions. Those types of regulated work require the applicable classification, specialty, or individual trade credential when required.

The broad scope of FIC work explains the variety of subjects included on the technical examination. A nonresidential agricultural building may require site preparation and excavation, concrete foundations, masonry, conventional or metal framing, manufactured trusses, roofing, siding, and multiple construction-safety practices.

Candidates should therefore approach Farm Improvement Contracting as a building-construction specialty with an agricultural application rather than as a single-trade examination.

    This federal construction-safety reference covers excavation safety, fall protection, ladders, scaffolds, tools, personal protective equipment, material handling, and other jobsite requirements applicable to construction operations.
  • International Building Code, 2021
    This building-code reference supports preparation involving nonresidential building requirements, structural systems, materials, fire and life-safety considerations, and other code provisions relevant to farm-building construction.
  • International Residential Code for One- and Two-Family Dwellings, 2021
    This construction-code reference provides technical information involving foundations, framing, roofs, structural components, materials, and other building systems useful for applicable examination subjects.
  • Carpentry and Building Construction, 2016

Straightforward trade-knowledge questions may be answered quickly, leaving additional time for code questions or calculations that require careful reference work.

The objective is not to memorize all eight references. A more practical goal is to understand the major concepts, recognize which book supports each subject, and develop enough familiarity with the references to locate detailed information efficiently when needed.

Exam Details

The Virginia Millwork and Finish Carpentry examination is administered through PSI for the Virginia Board for Contractors. The examination contains 30 questions, has a 90-minute time limit, and requires a minimum passing score of 70%, or 21 correct answers.

The official examination content outline is divided into eight subject areas:

  • Fabrication – 6 questions
  • Installation – 5 questions
  • Materials – 5 questions
  • Finishing – 4 questions
  • Hand Tools – 3 questions
  • Safety – 3 questions
  • Machines – 2 questions
  • Plans and Estimating – 2 questions

Fabrication is the largest individual category with 6 questions. Candidates should understand the methods used to cut, shape, assemble, and prepare millwork, cabinets, trim, and related finish carpentry components.

Installation and Materials each account for 5 questions. Installation questions can involve fitting, fastening, alignment, layout, and placement of finish carpentry components, while material questions can require candidates to recognize wood products, sheet goods, hardware, fasteners, adhesives, and other materials used in finish carpentry and cabinet work.

Finishing represents 4 questions. Candidates should be familiar with surface preparation, sanding, finishing materials, application techniques, and the steps used to produce a completed wood surface.

Hand Tools and Safety each represent 3 questions. Candidates should know the purpose and proper use of common finish carpentry tools while understanding the OSHA safety requirements that apply to construction work.

Machines and Plans and Estimating each account for 2 questions. Although smaller sections, both are important to a complete preparation plan because finish carpenters routinely use woodworking machinery and interpret dimensions, details, quantities, and specifications from construction documents.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Millwork and Finish Carpentry examination is an open book test. Candidates are permitted to use the approved references during the examination and must follow current PSI rules regarding allowable reference materials.

The 90-minute testing period provides an average of approximately three minutes per question. This gives candidates time to perform reference lookups when needed, but efficient navigation remains important. Spending several minutes searching through the wrong book can reduce the time available for more difficult questions.

The official reference list includes Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA), Finish Carpenter's Manual by Jim Tolpin, and The Complete Illustrated Guide to Furniture and Cabinet Construction.

A fabrication, trim, installation, or general finish carpentry question may direct the candidate toward the Finish Carpenter's Manual. Questions involving cabinetmaking, joinery, furniture construction, casework, and related woodworking concepts may be supported by The Complete Illustrated Guide to Furniture and Cabinet Construction. OSHA questions should direct attention to 29 CFR Part 1926.

PSI allows approved reference material to be highlighted, underlined, and indexed. Candidates should follow current testing rules when preparing books for the examination and should avoid unauthorized notes or loose materials.

Open-book preparation works best when candidates actively use their references during study. Learn the table of contents, index, terminology, diagrams, and major chapters so that a question can be matched to the appropriate reference quickly.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Board for Contractors. Contractor licenses consist of a license class and a classification or specialty that determines the type of work the business may perform. Finish Carpentry Contracting is identified by the specialty abbreviation FIN.

  1. Determine the appropriate Virginia contractor license class. Identify whether the business is pursuing a Class A, Class B, or Class C contractor license based on the scope and monetary level of work it intends to perform.
  2. Select the Finish Carpentry specialty. Request FIN when the business intends to perform work within Virginia's defined Finish Carpentry Contracting scope.
  3. Identify a Qualified Individual. Virginia requires a Qualified Individual for each classification or specialty listed on the contractor license.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirement. The Qualified Individual must have qualifying experience in the specialty. Virginia requires at least one year for Class C, three years for Class B, and five years for Class A.
  5. Complete the applicable contractor application requirements. Submit the information and documentation required by the Virginia Board for Contractors.
  6. Meet examination requirements. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the applicable technical examination requirement for the FIN specialty.
  7. Prepare for the Millwork and Finish Carpentry exam. Study Fabrication, Installation, Materials, Finishing, Hand Tools, Safety, Machines, and Plans and Estimating.
  8. Practice reference navigation. Become familiar with the Finish Carpenter's Manual, furniture and cabinet reference, and OSHA regulations before test day.
  9. Schedule testing through PSI. Follow the current registration and scheduling process for the Virginia specialty examination.
  10. Complete remaining licensing requirements. Satisfy the Board requirements associated with the contractor license class and specialty being requested.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Finish Carpentry Contracting as work involving the installation, repair, and finishing of cabinets, sash casing, door casing, wooden flooring, baseboards, countertops, and other millwork.

The FIN specialty does not include installation of ceramic tile, marble, or artificial or cultured stone. Those materials fall outside the defined Finish Carpentry Contracting scope.

Virginia also recognizes that the Residential Building and Commercial Building classifications and the Home Improvement Contracting and Commercial Improvement Contracting specialties provide for finish carpentry functions within their respective scopes.

The Virginia Board for Contractors licenses the business entity. The license class determines the monetary level of work the business may perform, while the classification or specialty determines the type of work authorized.

Every licensed contractor must identify a Qualified Individual for each specialty on the license. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the experience and prerequisite requirements associated with the requested designation.

Passing the Millwork and Finish Carpentry examination is an important technical qualification, but examination success alone does not automatically issue a Virginia contractor license. The business must complete all applicable Board licensing requirements.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive study plan should follow the official examination weighting. Begin with Fabrication, then devote substantial attention to Installation and Materials. Together, these three areas account for 16 of the 30 questions.

For Fabrication, study how finish carpentry components are measured, cut, shaped, joined, and assembled. Accuracy matters because small errors can affect fit, alignment, appearance, and installation quality.

Practice working with dimensions and layout. Finish carpentry frequently involves transferring measurements from an opening or plan to a piece of trim, cabinet component, countertop, casing, or other millwork.

Joinery should receive focused review. Cabinet and furniture construction can involve multiple methods for connecting wood components, and candidates should understand why different joints are used in different situations.

The Finish Carpenter's Manual is especially useful for practical installation and fabrication topics. Become familiar with sections covering interior trim, casings, moldings, cabinets, doors, and other finish carpentry work.

The Complete Illustrated Guide to Furniture and Cabinet Construction is useful for developing a deeper understanding of cabinet assemblies, case construction, doors, drawers, joinery, and woodworking processes.

For Installation, review methods for fitting finish components to actual field conditions. Walls, floors, ceilings, doors, and openings may not always be perfectly square, level, or plumb, so finish carpentry often requires careful fitting.

Door and window casing should be studied as complete assemblies. Candidates should understand layout, joints, fastening, reveals, fitting, and the relationship between the trim and the surrounding opening.

Baseboards and other moldings require similar attention. Practice recognizing the correct installation sequence and how inside corners, outside corners, joints, and changes in wall conditions affect the work.

Cabinet installation can involve layout, leveling, fastening, alignment, fitting to walls, countertop preparation, and coordination between adjacent units. Candidates should understand how cabinets are installed as a complete system rather than as isolated boxes.

Countertop work may involve measurement, fitting, joining, support, openings, edge treatment, and installation. Focus on the general principles described in the included references.

For Materials, review common solid-wood products, plywood, engineered wood products, sheet goods, veneers, hardware, fasteners, adhesives, and other materials associated with finish carpentry and cabinet construction.

Wood movement is an important finish carpentry concept. Changes in moisture can affect the dimensions of wood products, which can influence joints, fitting, installation, and finishing.

Material selection also affects appearance and performance. Different wood species and manufactured products have different properties that influence machining, fastening, finishing, and suitability for specific applications.

For Finishing, study surface preparation as carefully as the final coating. A high-quality finish depends on proper sanding, cleaning, preparation, and application.

Review the basic types of stains, sealers, finishes, and coatings discussed in the trade references. Candidates should understand the purpose of each stage rather than simply memorizing product names.

Sanding should be approached as a progressive process. Understanding abrasive selection, grain direction, surface defects, and preparation helps explain why certain finishing procedures produce better results.

Hand Tools represent three questions. Review measuring tools, layout tools, cutting tools, chisels, planes, hammers, nail sets, hand saws, and other common finish carpentry equipment.

Candidates should know both the purpose of a tool and the proper way to use it. Questions may focus on selecting the appropriate tool for a specific operation rather than simply identifying its name.

Machines account for two questions. Review common woodworking machinery and power equipment used in millwork and cabinet construction. Understand the function of each machine and the operations it is designed to perform.

Machine safety should be studied alongside machine operation. Cutting and shaping equipment can create serious hazards, so guarding, workpiece control, appropriate setup, and safe operating procedures are important.

Plans and Estimating account for two questions. Practice reading dimensions, elevations, sections, schedules, cabinet layouts, and other construction information relevant to finish work.

Estimating may involve determining quantities of trim, cabinets, flooring, molding, sheet goods, or other materials. Candidates should use consistent units and verify dimensions before completing calculations.

For Safety, study 29 CFR Part 1926. Finish carpenters may work with ladders, scaffolds, portable power tools, woodworking equipment, adhesives, coatings, heavy cabinets, and other construction materials.

Personal protective equipment should be included in preparation. Eye protection, hearing protection, respiratory considerations, and other protective measures may apply depending on the work being performed.

Ladder and scaffold safety are relevant because finish carpentry can involve work above floor level when installing crown molding, upper cabinets, tall trim, or other components.

Housekeeping also matters in finish work. Offcuts, cords, tools, fasteners, sawdust, and packaging can create trip or other hazards if work areas are not maintained properly.

A useful open-book strategy is to associate each examination subject with the most likely reference. Practical finish carpentry and installation questions should often direct attention toward the Finish Carpenter's Manual. Cabinet and furniture construction questions can point toward the illustrated cabinet reference. Safety questions should direct attention toward OSHA.

Practice under timed conditions. With 90 minutes for 30 questions, candidates average approximately three minutes per question. Straightforward trade questions should be answered efficiently so more time remains for detailed reference searches.

When a practice question is missed, identify the reason. The problem may result from unfamiliar terminology, choosing the wrong woodworking method, misunderstanding a material, using the wrong tool, or failing to locate the applicable OSHA requirement.

A strong Virginia Finish Carpentry exam preparation routine combines practical trade knowledge, fabrication and installation skills, material familiarity, finishing techniques, tool knowledge, plan reading, estimating, OSHA safety, and repeated reference navigation.

Important technical areas associated with the examination include:

  • General Electrical Knowledge
  • Wiring
  • Grounding
  • Power Supply
  • Detectors and Initiating Devices
  • Alarm Notification
  • General Fire Alarm Regulations

General Electrical Knowledge provides the foundation for understanding low-voltage fire alarm circuits. Candidates should be comfortable with basic electrical terminology, voltage, current, resistance, power, conductor characteristics, circuit behavior, and electrical safety principles.

Wiring is an important part of fire alarm installation. Candidates should understand conductor installation, cable routing, wiring methods, protection from physical damage, circuit identification, separation, and the electrical-code requirements that apply to fire alarm circuits.

Grounding requires candidates to understand the relationship between fire alarm equipment and the electrical grounding system. Grounding and bonding provisions can affect equipment installation, circuit protection, and overall system reliability.

Power Supply includes understanding how fire alarm systems receive normal and secondary power. Fire alarm systems must continue to perform important life-safety functions under conditions anticipated by the applicable code and standard.

Detectors and Initiating Devices involve the equipment used to detect fire-related conditions or manually initiate an alarm. Candidates should understand the purpose, placement concepts, application, and operation of common initiating devices.

Alarm Notification involves devices and systems used to alert building occupants and other parties when an alarm condition occurs. Candidates should be familiar with audible, visible, and other notification concepts addressed by NFPA 72.

General Regulations can include system installation, inspection, testing, maintenance, documentation, and other requirements governing fire alarm system performance and reliability.

Approved examination references may be prepared according to current PSI rules. Candidates should become familiar with the testing requirements governing highlighting, underlining, indexing, and permanent tabs before preparing books for exam day.

An open-book exam still requires significant preparation. Fire alarm questions can involve terminology that appears in both electrical and fire alarm standards. Candidates should know whether a question is primarily asking about an electrical wiring requirement or a specialized fire alarm requirement before deciding which reference to open.

For example, a question involving the installation of fire alarm circuit conductors may require the National Electrical Code. A question involving detector application, notification appliances, supervising stations, emergency communications, inspection, testing, or maintenance is more likely to require NFPA 72.

Practice navigating both books under timed conditions. Learn the table of contents, index, major Articles and Chapters, defined terms, tables, and frequently used sections. The National Electrical Code establishes many of the electrical installation requirements, while NFPA 72 addresses the specialized performance and operation of fire alarm and signaling systems.

Begin with General Electrical Knowledge. Review voltage, current, resistance, power, electrical circuits, conductor concepts, and electrical terminology. Understanding these fundamentals makes it easier to interpret wiring and power-supply questions.

Next, study fire alarm wiring. Become familiar with the NEC provisions specifically addressing fire alarm circuits. Candidates should understand that different circuit types and installation conditions can affect the wiring methods and protection requirements that apply.

Conductor protection should receive focused review. Wiring can pass through walls, ceilings, framing, mechanical spaces, and other portions of a building where physical conditions influence installation requirements.

Practice identifying whether a question relates to cable type, conductor routing, protection, support, separation, circuit classification, or termination. Identifying the specific issue before looking up the code can significantly improve navigation speed.

Grounding should be studied as part of the complete electrical installation. Candidates should understand basic grounding and bonding concepts and how equipment grounding relates to the reliability and safety of installed systems.

Power supplies are critical to fire alarm operation. Review the concepts of primary and secondary power and understand why a fire alarm system must have the power needed to perform its required functions.

NFPA 72 should be a central part of study for initiating devices. Review smoke detection, heat detection, manual fire alarm boxes, waterflow-related initiation, supervisory devices, and other equipment used to initiate or report system conditions.

Candidates should understand the difference between alarm, supervisory, and trouble conditions. These terms have specific meanings in fire alarm systems and can affect how signals are processed and annunciated.

Detector questions can involve application and installation. Rather than memorizing individual statements, study how detector type, environment, location, ceiling configuration, and system design influence placement and performance.

Notification appliances are another important study area. Review audible and visible notification concepts and understand how fire alarm systems communicate emergency information to occupants.

Visible notification requires familiarity with the purpose and application of visual signaling devices. Audible notification requires understanding of sound-based occupant notification and the performance concepts addressed by NFPA 72.

Candidates should also review notification appliance circuits and how field devices relate to the fire alarm control equipment and power supplies.

Fire alarm control units serve as a central part of many systems. Candidates should understand the general relationship among initiating devices, control equipment, notification appliances, power supplies, and monitoring functions.

Study supervising station systems and the basic purposes of off-premises monitoring. Candidates should understand how signals can be transmitted from protected premises to locations responsible for receiving and processing those signals.

Emergency communications systems are also addressed by NFPA 72. Candidates should become familiar with the terminology and organization of these provisions so they can locate the appropriate material when a question involves emergency messages or mass notification concepts.

Inspection, testing, and maintenance should receive substantial attention. Fire alarm systems must remain operational throughout their service life, and NFPA 72 includes requirements addressing how systems and components are inspected, tested, documented, and maintained.

Practice recognizing whether a question concerns initial acceptance, periodic inspection, functional testing, maintenance, recordkeeping, or system impairment. Each of these topics has a different purpose within the overall fire alarm lifecycle.

System documentation should also be included in preparation. Fire alarm work can involve drawings, specifications, equipment information, test records, and other documentation necessary to demonstrate system design and performance.

Detection, notification, system operation, signaling, testing, and maintenance should generally direct attention toward NFPA 72.

Wood flooring introduces moisture and finishing considerations, while tile work requires familiarity with industry installation standards. Successful preparation should reflect those differences.

Exam Details

The Virginia Flooring and Floor Covering Contracting examination is the technical specialty examination associated with the FLR designation. The examination is administered through PSI for the Virginia Board for Contractors.

The examination contains 50 questions, allows 120 minutes for completion, and requires a minimum passing score of 70%, or 35 correct answers.

The official content outline is divided into six major categories:

  • Ceramic Floor Tile and Stone – 16 questions
  • Resilient Flooring – 6 questions
  • Wood Flooring – 10 questions
  • Carpeting – 8 questions
  • Estimating Materials – 5 questions
  • Safety – 5 questions

Ceramic Floor Tile and Stone is the largest examination area. Candidates should devote significant preparation time to tile substrates, surface preparation, setting materials, installation methods, layout, grout, movement accommodation, cutting, and recognized industry practices.

Wood Flooring is another major category. Preparation should include moisture considerations, subfloor conditions, flooring layout, installation, fastening, sanding, finishing, and practical hardwood-floor techniques.

Carpeting requires familiarity with measuring, layout, seams, cushion, tack strips, stretching, fitting, floor preparation, and installation procedures. Resilient Flooring requires knowledge of substrates, adhesives, layout, cutting, seams, and installation techniques.

Estimating Materials tests the candidate's ability to work with dimensions and flooring quantities. Safety requires familiarity with construction safety requirements relevant to flooring work, tools, materials, and jobsite conditions.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Flooring and Floor Covering Contracting examination is an open book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing allowable references and following current PSI rules governing reference materials.

Approved references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted under PSI reference rules, while removable tabs are not allowed. Candidates should prepare their books in accordance with current testing requirements.

The examination provides 120 minutes for 50 questions, giving candidates an average of approximately two minutes and twenty-four seconds per question. That makes reference navigation an important part of preparation.

A candidate who knows a technical subject but spends several minutes searching the wrong reference can lose valuable testing time. The course therefore emphasizes identifying the type of question first and then selecting the most appropriate reference.

For example, questions about tile installation standards may direct attention toward the ANSI reference. Questions about recognized ceramic tile installation assemblies may point toward the ceramic tile handbook. Practical tile-setting subjects may be reinforced through Setting Tile.

Hardwood questions can direct candidates toward Hardwood Floors: Laying, Sanding, and Finishing. General flooring concepts may be supported by Stanley Complete Flooring or Builder’s Guide to Floors. Safety questions should direct attention toward OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926.

The listed preparation materials include ANSI A108/A118/A136 August 2024. The PSI examination reference list identifies ANSI A108/A118/A136.1:2017 as the examination reference edition on which applicable questions are based. Candidates using the newer August 2024 edition should study with awareness of that edition distinction.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Board for Contractors. Contractor licenses are issued by license class and classification or specialty. The license class determines the monetary level of contracting work, while the classification or specialty determines the type of work authorized.

  1. Determine the appropriate contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select the FLR specialty. Choose Flooring and Floor Covering Contracting when the business intends to perform work within Virginia's defined flooring scope.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. The business must designate a Qualified Individual for each classification or specialty.
  4. Meet applicable experience requirements. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the experience requirements associated with the license class being pursued.
  5. Complete required pre-license education. Virginia requires eight hours of Board-approved pre-license education for new Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor applicants.
  6. Obtain pre-approval for the FLR examination. Virginia identifies FLR as a specialty requiring pre-approval and successful completion of a technical exam.
  7. Prepare for the technical examination. Study ceramic tile, stone, resilient flooring, hardwood, carpeting, estimating, and OSHA safety.
  8. Practice open-book reference navigation. Become familiar with the books and standards associated with each major examination subject.
  9. Complete the applicable examination requirements. Follow Virginia and PSI procedures for the specialty and license class being pursued.
  10. Complete the contractor application process. Submit the required information and satisfy the remaining Virginia Board for Contractors requirements.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Flooring and Floor Covering Contracting as the installation, repair, improvement, or removal of materials commonly used in the flooring industry.

The scope includes wood and wood-composite flooring, tack strips and other carpet securing products, vinyl, linoleum, ceramic, marble, stone, and other types of tile.

The FLR specialty also includes installation or replacement of subflooring, leveling products, and other materials necessary to facilitate installation of the finished flooring or floor covering.

Virginia specifically excludes installation, repair, or removal of floor joists and other structural components of the flooring system from the FLR specialty.

Virginia contractor licenses are issued to business entities and sole proprietors. A Qualified Individual demonstrates the technical qualifications associated with the requested classification or specialty.

Virginia identifies FLR as a specialty requiring pre-approval and successful completion of a technical examination. Passing the exam is one component of the licensing process and does not by itself issue a Virginia contractor license.
