Start with substrate preparation. Flooring performance depends heavily on the condition of the surface beneath the finished material. Candidates should understand leveling, cleanliness, stability, moisture-related concerns, and compatibility with the selected flooring system.

For tile work, review mortars, adhesives, grout, layout, cutting, setting, movement accommodation, and recognized installation methods. Use the ANSI reference to become comfortable with technical standards and the ceramic tile handbook to reinforce installation assemblies and methods.

Use Setting Tile to strengthen practical understanding of tile installation. Knowing how a process is performed can make it easier to interpret technical questions about materials, tools, preparation, or installation sequence.

For Wood Flooring, concentrate on moisture conditions, substrate preparation, layout, flooring direction, fastening, sanding, and finishing. Hardwood flooring requires careful preparation because wood responds to environmental conditions and moisture changes.

Review sanding as a complete process rather than an isolated task. Candidates should understand surface preparation, equipment, abrasive progression, and how sanding affects the final finish.

For Carpeting, study room measurement, layout, carpet direction, cushion, tack strips, seams, stretching, fitting, and trimming. Carpet questions may combine installation knowledge with estimating concepts.

Read estimating questions carefully and keep units consistent. A correct formula can still lead to the wrong answer if measurements are converted incorrectly or an installation condition is overlooked.

Review personal protective equipment, hand and power tools, electrical safety, material handling, housekeeping, and other OSHA concepts relevant to flooring work.

The problem may be an unfamiliar flooring term, incorrect installation method, calculation error, misunderstanding of a material, or difficulty finding the applicable information in a reference. Exam Details

The Virginia Flooring and Floor Covering Contracting examination is a technical specialty examination for Qualified Individuals seeking the FLR designation. Virginia identifies FLR as one of the specialties requiring pre-approval and successful completion of an approved technical examination.

The examination contains 50 scored questions, provides 120 minutes for completion, and requires a minimum passing score of 70%, or 35 correct answers.

The major examination areas include:

  • Ceramic Floor Tile and Stone
  • Resilient Flooring
  • Wood Flooring
  • Carpeting
  • Estimating Materials
  • Safety

Ceramic tile and stone make up a substantial part of the technical knowledge required for the FLR examination. Candidates should study recognized installation methods, substrates, mortars, adhesives, grout, movement accommodation, layout, cutting, setting procedures, and material requirements.

Wood-flooring preparation should include layout, substrate conditions, moisture considerations, fastening, installation techniques, sanding, and finishing. Carpet and resilient-flooring preparation should include surface preparation, measuring, layout, seams, adhesives, cushion, tack strips, and installation procedures.

Estimating is another important part of preparation. Candidates should be comfortable calculating square footage, determining material quantities, interpreting dimensions, and applying the information presented in trade scenarios.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Board for Contractors. Contractor licenses consist of a license class and a classification or specialty. Flooring and Floor Covering Contracting is identified by the specialty abbreviation FLR.

  1. Determine the appropriate contractor license class. Virginia contractor licenses are issued as Class A, Class B, or Class C, with the class determining the monetary level of contracting work that may be performed.
  2. Select the FLR specialty. Request Flooring and Floor Covering Contracting when the business intends to perform work within Virginia's defined flooring specialty.
  3. Designate a Qualified Individual. The business must identify a Qualified Individual for each requested classification or specialty.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirements. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the experience standards associated with the applicable contractor license class.
  5. Complete applicable pre-license requirements. New Virginia contractor applicants must satisfy the education and application requirements established by the Board.
  6. Receive exam approval. FLR is identified by Virginia as a specialty requiring pre-approval and successful completion of a technical examination.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Flooring and Floor Covering Contracting as installation, repair, improvement, or removal of materials commonly used in the flooring industry.

The FLR specialty includes wood and wood-composite flooring, tack strips and other products used to secure carpet, vinyl and linoleum, ceramic, marble, stone, and other types of tile.

Virginia's definition also includes installation or replacement of subflooring, leveling products, and other materials necessary to facilitate installation of flooring or floor coverings.

The specialty does not include installation, repair, or removal of floor joists or other structural components of the flooring system. Structural work beyond the FLR scope requires the appropriate contractor authorization.

The Virginia Board for Contractors licenses the business entity. The contractor license class establishes the monetary level of work the business may undertake, while the classification or specialty determines the type of work the contractor is authorized to perform.

Virginia identifies FLR as one of the specialties for which Qualified Individuals must successfully complete an approved technical examination in addition to meeting applicable experience requirements.

Passing the FLR examination is only one part of obtaining the contractor license. Applicants must complete the full Board licensing process before performing work that requires a Virginia contractor license.

What does FRM mean in Virginia contractor licensing?

FRM is the Virginia Board for Contractors abbreviation for Framing Contractor.

What type of work does the Virginia Framing Contractor specialty cover?

The specialty covers construction, removal, repair, or improvement of framing and rough carpentry necessary for framed structures, including installation and repair of individual components of framing systems.

Is the Virginia Framing Contractor exam open book?

Yes. Virginia contractor specialty examinations administered by PSI are open book. Candidates must bring their own permitted reference materials.

What books are included in this package?

Can I write notes inside the exam books?

No. Virginia PSI examination rules require references to remain otherwise unmarked, and written notes are not permitted.

Does the FRM qualified individual need experience?

Yes. Virginia requires at least one year of applicable experience for a Class C qualified individual, three years for Class B, and five years for Class A.

Is pre-license education required for a new Virginia contractor license?

Yes. New Virginia contractor applicants must complete eight hours of Board-approved pre-license education in addition to satisfying applicable examination and licensing requirements.

Prepare for the Virginia Home Improvement Contractor examination with an online exam prep course focused on the construction knowledge, technical references, and open-book navigation skills associated with the Virginia Home Improvement Contracting specialty (HIC). The course provides a structured way to study a broad residential construction examination covering subjects such as concrete, masonry, carpentry, drywall, siding, roofing, insulation, painting, safety, windows, and doors.

Virginia Home Improvement Contracting covers repairs and improvements to dwellings and townhouses, as well as structures annexed to those dwellings or townhouses, within the scope established by Virginia contractor regulations. Because HIC encompasses several construction disciplines, candidates preparing for the technical examination need to be comfortable moving between multiple trade subjects rather than concentrating on one specialty.

The Virginia Home Improvement Contractor Online Exam Prep Course helps organize those subjects into a more manageable preparation process. Instead of approaching numerous code books, construction manuals, standards, and trade references without direction, candidates can focus their study on the knowledge areas represented on the HIC examination and develop stronger habits for navigating the books associated with those subjects.

The examination is open book, making familiarity with the reference materials an important part of preparation. Candidates should understand not only construction concepts but also which reference is most likely to contain the information needed for a particular question. Practicing this process before exam day can help candidates use their available examination time more efficiently.

The course is intended for candidates who want an organized, trade-focused approach to Virginia HIC preparation. Study should combine construction knowledge with repeated reference navigation so that important chapters, standards, indexes, and technical sections become increasingly familiar.

Exam Details

The Virginia Home Improvement Contracting Examination is the technical specialty examination associated with the HIC designation. Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation through the Board for Contractors, and PSI administers the specialty examination.

  • Specialty: Home Improvement Contracting
  • Specialty Abbreviation: HIC
  • Number of Questions: 50
  • Time Allowed: 120 minutes
  • Passing Score: 70%, or 35 correct answers
  • Testing Provider: PSI

The examination covers a wide range of residential construction subjects. The published content outline includes:

  • Concrete: 4 questions
  • Masonry: 4 questions
  • Painting and Wall Covering: 4 questions
  • Drywall: 4 questions
  • Rough Carpentry and Framing: 5 questions
  • Siding: 5 questions
  • Finish Carpentry: 5 questions
  • Roofing: 5 questions
  • Insulation: 5 questions
  • Safety: 5 questions
  • Windows and Doors: 4 questions

The content distribution demonstrates why broad preparation matters. No single subject dominates the entire exam. Candidates need working knowledge across multiple residential construction trades and should be prepared to identify which reference applies when a technical question requires additional information.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Home Improvement Contracting examination is an open book test. Candidates must bring their own allowable references because the testing center does not provide the books used for the examination.

PSI permits allowable reference materials to be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination. Permanent tabs are permitted. Removable tabs and flags are not permitted. Study guides are not permitted as exam-room references, and candidates must follow the applicable PSI rules governing reference materials.

The open-book format makes reference-navigation practice an important part of preparation. Candidates have 120 minutes to answer 50 questions, which provides an average of approximately two minutes and twenty-four seconds per question. Searching an unfamiliar book without knowing where to begin can consume valuable testing time.

A more effective method is to identify the subject first. A workplace-safety question may direct you toward OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926. A residential code question may require the International Residential Code. A masonry question may point toward Modern Masonry, while drywall information may be located in the Gypsum Construction Handbook.

Practice this process while studying. Determine the subject, choose the most relevant reference, use the index or table of contents, locate the applicable section, and carefully read the surrounding material. Technical questions may depend on conditions, exceptions, measurements, or specific installation requirements, so finding the correct page is only part of the process.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered through the Board for Contractors. Contractor licenses are issued to business entities and sole proprietors and consist of a license class together with one or more classifications or specialty designations.

  1. Determine the contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select the Home Improvement Contracting specialty. HIC identifies the applicable specialty for qualifying home improvement work.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. The contractor business must identify a Qualified Individual for the applicable specialty.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirements. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the experience requirements associated with the requested license class and specialty.
  5. Complete required pre-license education. New Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor license applicants must complete eight hours of approved pre-license education.
  6. Complete the HIC technical examination requirement. Follow the Board for Contractors and PSI procedures applicable to the specialty examination.
  7. Complete additional requirements associated with the license class. Virginia has separate requirements that may apply depending on whether the business is pursuing Class A, Class B, or Class C licensing.
  8. Submit the contractor license application. Complete the Virginia Board for Contractors application process and provide the required supporting documentation.

Passing the HIC technical examination is one part of the contractor licensing process. Exam completion alone does not issue a Virginia contractor license.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Home Improvement Contracting as the service providing repairs or improvements to dwellings and townhouses as defined in the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code, or structures annexed to those dwellings or townhouses.

The Residential Building Contractor classification also provides for the home improvement function. The HIC specialty does not provide for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or gas-fitting functions.

The HIC specialty also does not include new-construction functions beyond the existing building structure except for decks, patios, driveways, and utility outbuildings that do not require a permit under the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code.

Virginia contractor licenses contain both a license class and a classification or specialty. Candidates pursuing HIC should therefore understand that qualifying for the specialty is only one component of the complete contractor licensing process.

New Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor license applicants are also required to complete eight hours of Board-approved pre-license education. This business-focused licensing requirement is separate from technical preparation for the HIC specialty examination.

Reference Books

  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    Provides federal construction-industry safety requirements covering subjects such as personal protective equipment, tools, fall hazards, electrical safety, ladders, scaffolding, material handling, and general construction-site safety.
  • International Residential Code for One- and Two-Family Dwellings, 2021
    Provides residential code requirements for one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses. It supports preparation involving residential construction provisions, building components, structural requirements, roofing, openings, and other code-regulated work.
  • Carpentry and Building Construction, 2016
    Covers carpentry fundamentals, building materials, framing, construction systems, tools, layout, structural components, and practical residential construction methods.
  • The Contractor's Guide to Quality Concrete Construction - 4th Edition
    Supports preparation involving concrete materials, placement, preparation, finishing, curing, and quality concrete construction practices.
  • Painting & Decorating Craftsman's Manual and Textbook, Eighth Edition, 1995
    Covers surface preparation, painting materials, coatings, application methods, tools, decorating practices, and related finishing procedures.
  • Modern Masonry - Brick, Block, Stone, Clois E. Kicklighter, 10th Edition
    Provides practical and technical information involving brick, concrete block, stone, mortar, masonry tools, layout, and common construction techniques.
  • Standard Practice for Installation of Rigid Poly(Vinyl Chloride) (PVC) Siding and Soffit - ASTM D 4756
    Provides standardized practices associated with rigid PVC siding and soffit installation, including installation procedures and related technical considerations.
  • Insulation Handbook, 2001
    Supports preparation involving insulation materials, thermal concepts, installation practices, residential applications, and building-envelope considerations.
  • Gypsum Construction Handbook, 7th Edition
    Provides information on gypsum products, drywall systems, walls, ceilings, fastening, installation, joints, finishing, and other gypsum construction methods.
  • Finish Carpenter's Manual, Jim Tolpin, 1993
    Focuses on finish-carpentry methods, trim work, fitting, measuring, layout, interior woodworking, tools, and practical residential finishing techniques.
  • ICC A117.1-2017 Standard for Accessible and Usable Buildings and Facilities
    Provides technical accessibility criteria involving dimensions, clearances, accessible routes, doors, maneuvering spaces, and other building elements associated with accessibility and usability.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive HIC study plan should divide preparation into the examination's major construction categories. This approach helps candidates connect each subject with the appropriate technical reference.

For concrete, review materials, preparation, placement, finishing, curing, and quality-control practices. For masonry, study brick, block, stone, mortar, layout, tools, and typical residential masonry procedures.

For painting and wall covering, review surface preparation, coatings, tools, application techniques, and finishing procedures. For drywall, become familiar with gypsum products, fasteners, wall and ceiling systems, joints, finishing methods, and installation practices.

Rough carpentry and framing requires familiarity with framing terminology, structural members, floor and wall systems, roof construction, layout, fastening, and common residential building practices. The general carpentry reference is also useful when studying windows, doors, and other building components.

For siding, review installation practices, fastening, layout, exterior preparation, and the technical requirements associated with rigid PVC siding and soffit. For finish carpentry, focus on trim, fitting, measurement, interior woodworking, doors, and finishing techniques.

For roofing, review residential code provisions and construction practices associated with residential roof systems. For insulation, study insulation materials, thermal principles, placement, and installation considerations.

The safety portion of the exam should include regular practice with OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926. Instead of attempting to memorize the entire reference, become comfortable using its organization and locating requirements involving common construction hazards and safe work practices.

For windows and doors, study openings, framing considerations, installation, dimensions, residential code requirements, and applicable accessibility criteria.

During practice, use the technical references instead of relying only on memory. Start by identifying which trade or code subject the question addresses, then select the most likely book and locate the supporting material. Repeated reference-navigation practice can help make the open-book format more manageable.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps Virginia Home Improvement Contractor candidates organize a broad technical examination into focused study categories. The HIC exam combines many areas of residential construction, and an organized study structure can make it easier to work through those subjects systematically.

The online exam prep course supports trade-focused review involving concrete, masonry, painting, drywall, framing, siding, finish carpentry, roofing, insulation, safety, windows, and doors. Candidates can use the technical references alongside their preparation to strengthen both construction knowledge and familiarity with the books.

Reference navigation is especially important for an open-book examination. 1 Exam Prep encourages candidates to develop a repeatable process: recognize the topic, select the appropriate reference, locate the applicable section, and carefully interpret the information in relation to the question.

Practice-oriented preparation can also help candidates identify weaker subject areas. When a question is missed, return to the relevant reference and determine whether the issue was unfamiliar terminology, a technical concept, an installation method, a code requirement, or difficulty navigating the book.

The goal is to develop stronger trade knowledge, better reference-navigation habits, and a more organized study approach so candidates can prepare for the Virginia HIC examination with greater familiarity and confidence.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Virginia Home Improvement Contractor specialty?

Home Improvement Contracting, abbreviated HIC, covers qualifying repairs and improvements to dwellings, townhouses, and structures annexed to them within the scope established by Virginia contractor regulations.

Is the Virginia HIC exam open book?

Yes. The Virginia Home Improvement Contracting examination is an open-book test. Candidates must bring their own allowable references and comply with PSI rules governing examination materials.

How many questions are on the Virginia HIC exam?

The examination contains 50 questions.

How much time is allowed?

Candidates have 120 minutes to complete the HIC examination.

What score is required to pass?

The minimum passing score is 70%, or 35 correct answers out of 50 questions.

What subjects are covered on the HIC exam?

The examination covers Concrete, Masonry, Painting and Wall Covering, Drywall, Rough Carpentry and Framing, Siding, Finish Carpentry, Roofing, Insulation, Safety, and Windows and Doors.

Does the examination use the 2021 International Residential Code?

Yes. PSI states that applicable ICC code questions are based on the 2021 code edition, including the International Residential Code.

Can I use highlighted books during the exam?

Allowable references may be highlighted and underlined before the examination. Permanent tabs are also permitted, while removable tabs are not allowed.

Does the HIC specialty include electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or gas fitting?

No. Virginia's HIC specialty does not provide for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or gas-fitting functions.

Does passing the HIC exam automatically issue a Virginia contractor license?

No. Passing the technical specialty examination is one component of the licensing process. The contracting business must also satisfy the requirements applicable to its license class, Qualified Individual, pre-license education, application, and supporting documentation.

How can an online exam prep course help with an open-book test?

An organized course can help candidates review the construction subjects represented on the exam while developing familiarity with the technical references. Practicing how to connect questions with the correct books can support more efficient reference navigation during a timed open-book examination.

Why prepare with the exam references instead of relying only on memorization?

The HIC examination covers multiple technical construction subjects. Using the references throughout preparation can help candidates understand where information is located and practice interpreting code provisions, standards, and trade guidance in context.

Exam Details

The ICC Fire Inspector II - 67 examination contains 50 multiple-choice questions and has a 2-hour time limit.

The official ICC examination outline divides the exam into four major content areas:

  • General Inspection Administration – 20%
  • General Provisions for Fire Safety – 36%
  • Occupancies – 22%
  • Regulated Materials and Processes – 22%

General Provisions for Fire Safety is the largest content area at 36%. Candidates should devote substantial preparation time to means of egress, construction types, fire-protection equipment and system readiness, emergency access, fire-flow information, emergency planning, fire-protection inspections, exposures, and comparing approved plans with installed fire-protection systems.

Occupancies account for 22% of the examination. Candidates should be prepared to identify occupancy classifications, calculate allowable occupant loads, and conduct fire-safety inspections for different occupancy types.

Regulated Materials and Processes also represent 22%. This section includes industrial and commercial processes, storage and handling of regulated materials, and evaluation of interior finishes, furnishings, and decorative materials for code compliance.

Prepare for the Virginia Journeyman Natural Gasfitter examination with an online exam prep course designed to help you organize your study, strengthen technical gasfitting knowledge, and become more efficient using the references associated with the open-book examination. This course focuses on the technical and Virginia regulatory topics candidates need to understand while building a practical study routine around gas piping, pipe sizing, controls, testing, and code navigation.

The Virginia Journeyman Natural Gasfitter credential is an individual tradesman license regulated by the Virginia Board for Contractors through the Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation. Candidates seeking this credential must satisfy the applicable qualification requirements, receive examination approval, successfully complete the required test, and meet the remaining licensing requirements established by Virginia.

The examination covers both technical natural gasfitting subjects and Virginia tradesman regulations. Natural and LP gas piping and pipe sizing make up a substantial portion of the test, so candidates should be prepared to work with fuel-gas system requirements, piping materials, installation methods, sizing tables, valves, regulators, controls, and testing procedures.

The Virginia Journeyman Natural Gasfitter Online Exam Prep course is organized around the listed reference materials: the Virginia Board for Contractors Individual License and Certification Regulations, the International Fuel Gas Code, 2021, and NFPA 58 - Standard for Liquid Petroleum Gas Code, 2014. These references support study across both regulatory requirements and technical gas-system knowledge.

Because the examination is open book, candidates should learn how to use the references efficiently rather than relying on the books only when they encounter an unfamiliar question. Understanding how each reference is organized, where major topics are located, and how to use indexes and technical tables can make study more productive and improve reference-navigation skills before exam day.

Exam Details

The Virginia Journeyman Natural Gasfitter examination is administered by PSI for the Virginia Board for Contractors. Candidates must receive approval through the Board before scheduling the examination.

The current Journeyman/Master Natural Gasfitter examination portion contains 50 items. Journeyman candidates must answer 35 questions correctly to meet the Journeyman passing requirement. Candidates receive 150 minutes to complete the examination.

The examination content is divided between Virginia regulatory topics and technical natural gasfitting knowledge. The current content outline includes:

  • Standards of Practice: 3 items.
  • Standards of Conduct: 2 items.
  • Renewal and Reinstatement: 2 items.
  • Definitions: 1 item.
  • Qualification for Licensure: 1 item.
  • Revocation of Licensure: 1 item.
  • Natural and LP Gas Piping: 18 items.
  • Pipe Sizing: 14 items.
  • Gas Piping Controls: 5 items.
  • Testing: 3 items.

Natural and LP Gas Piping and Pipe Sizing together account for 32 of the 50 examination items. These subjects should receive substantial attention during preparation. Candidates should understand piping systems and know how to work with the technical tables and provisions used to determine proper pipe sizing.

Gas Piping Controls and Testing are additional technical areas. Questions can involve valves, regulators, shutoff devices, pressure-related components, system controls, and procedures used to test and verify gas piping installations.

The Virginia regulatory portion covers responsibilities that apply to licensed tradesmen. Candidates should review professional standards, licensing qualifications, definitions, renewal and reinstatement provisions, and disciplinary requirements rather than concentrating exclusively on technical code material.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Journeyman Natural Gasfitter examination is an open book test. Candidates may bring qualifying reference materials into the examination when those materials comply with current PSI requirements.

Qualifying references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before testing. Permanent tabs may be used to organize approved reference materials. Candidates should make sure their books comply with the testing provider's current rules regarding markings, tabs, notes, and reference preparation before arriving for the examination.

The open-book format does not eliminate the need to study. Candidates have 150 minutes for 50 questions, providing an average of three minutes per item. Some questions may be completed quickly, but technical lookups and pipe-sizing problems can require more time.

Efficient reference navigation can therefore be an important part of preparation. Instead of opening every book for every question, candidates should learn to identify the subject first and select the reference that is most likely to contain the answer.

A question about standards of practice, professional conduct, renewal, or licensing qualifications may direct the candidate toward the Virginia Board for Contractors Individual License and Certification Regulations. A question involving piping systems, sizing, controls, appliances, or testing may require the International Fuel Gas Code. LP-gas-related provisions may involve NFPA 58.

The online exam prep course encourages candidates to practice this process repeatedly. Recognize the topic, select the appropriate reference, locate the relevant chapter or table, and review the supporting requirement. This helps build code-navigation familiarity alongside technical knowledge.

Licensing Steps

Virginia Journeyman Natural Gasfitter licensing is an individual tradesman licensing process. Candidates must meet the applicable Virginia Board for Contractors requirements before receiving authorization to take the examination.

  1. Select the appropriate credential. Confirm that the Journeyman Natural Gas Fitter Provider license matches the work and licensing level you intend to pursue.
  2. Review Virginia qualification requirements. Applicants must meet an applicable combination of practical experience, formal training, education, apprenticeship, or other qualifying credentials.
  3. Document practical natural gasfitting experience. Candidates must provide documentation supporting the experience required for their qualification pathway.
  4. Document training or education when applicable. Applicants using formal vocational training or another educational pathway must submit the required supporting records.
  5. Submit the applicable tradesman application. The Virginia Board for Contractors reviews the applicant's qualifications as part of the approval process.
  6. Receive examination approval. Candidates must receive authorization from the Board before scheduling the Natural Gasfitter examination.
  7. Prepare for the examination. Study technical gasfitting subjects, Virginia regulations, and the applicable reference books.
  8. Schedule the examination through PSI. After Board approval, candidates can complete the applicable PSI scheduling process.
  9. Take the Journeyman Natural Gasfitter examination. Candidates must meet the Journeyman passing requirement.
  10. Complete the remaining licensing process. The Virginia Board for Contractors handles license issuance after the applicable requirements have been satisfied.

State Requirements

Virginia regulates Natural Gas Fitter Providers as individual tradesmen. Applicants must demonstrate that they meet the knowledge, skills, abilities, education, training, and practical experience requirements applicable to the license they are seeking.

The Virginia Board for Contractors reviews the applicant's qualification documentation before authorizing the examination. Candidates should use the pathway that accurately reflects their actual experience, training, apprenticeship, education, or licensing background.

Current Virginia regulations provide qualification pathways that combine formal vocational training with practical experience for Natural Gas Fitter Provider applicants. Documentation must support the specific pathway selected by the applicant.

The Board also recognizes other qualifying circumstances established under Virginia tradesman regulations. These can include approved apprenticeship-related qualifications and certain licensing situations when the applicable requirements are met.

Pre-approval is required before an applicant can take the Virginia Journeyman Natural Gasfitter examination. Candidates should therefore complete the application and eligibility process before attempting to schedule the examination through PSI.

After licensure, Natural Gasfitter licensees must maintain their credentials in accordance with Virginia renewal requirements. Applicable continuing education requirements must be completed through Board-approved education providers when required for renewal.

The online exam prep course supports examination preparation but does not replace Virginia's licensing eligibility requirements. Candidates remain responsible for satisfying the applicable experience, education, training, examination, application, and renewal requirements.

Reference Books

  • Virginia Board for Contractors, Individual License and Certification Regulations
    This regulatory reference supports preparation for Virginia-specific examination subjects such as standards of practice, standards of conduct, renewal and reinstatement, definitions, qualifications for licensure, disciplinary provisions, and other individual tradesman requirements.
  • International Fuel Gas Code, 2021
    This primary technical fuel-gas reference covers piping materials, system installation, pipe sizing, appliance connections, controls, regulators, valves, combustion air, venting, testing, and other fuel-gas requirements. Candidates should become familiar with the book's tables, chapter structure, and index during preparation.
  • NFPA 58 - Standard for Liquid Petroleum Gas Code, 2014
    This technical reference addresses LP-gas systems, containers, piping, equipment, installation, storage, protection, and safety requirements. It can support preparation for LP-gas concepts included within the Natural and LP Gas Piping portion of the examination.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive Virginia Journeyman Natural Gasfitter study plan should reflect the weight of the examination topics. Natural and LP Gas Piping and Pipe Sizing make up most of the technical portion, so candidates should spend significant time developing both conceptual knowledge and reference-navigation skills in these areas.

Natural and LP Gas Piping includes a broad range of fuel-gas system concepts. Review piping materials, fittings, joining methods, installation conditions, supports, protection, regulators, valves, appliance connections, system configuration, and related installation requirements.

When studying a piping concept, locate the corresponding material in the International Fuel Gas Code rather than relying only on summaries. This helps connect the technical idea with the language and organization of the actual reference.

Pipe Sizing represents 14 examination items and should receive dedicated practice. Candidates need to recognize the information provided in a sizing problem, determine which sizing method or table applies, and accurately read the applicable values.

Practice locating sizing tables repeatedly. Candidates should become familiar with how piping length, gas demand, pressure, and system conditions affect table selection and pipe-size determination. Building a repeatable process can be more useful than memorizing the answer to individual examples.

Start a sizing problem by identifying the conditions presented. Determine what information is necessary, select the applicable code table, and then verify the result carefully. Practicing this sequence can help make sizing problems more manageable under exam conditions.

Gas Piping Controls preparation should include regulators, valves, shutoff devices, controls, pressure-related equipment, and safety components. Candidates should know the purpose of these devices as well as the code provisions affecting where and how they are used.

Testing should include gas-piping pressure tests, system verification, and applicable procedures for confirming the condition of the installation. Testing questions can depend on specific code language, making careful reading and accurate reference use important.

The Virginia regulatory material should remain part of the weekly study schedule. Review standards of practice, standards of conduct, qualifications, definitions, renewal and reinstatement, and disciplinary provisions. These topics may be easier to locate during the exam when candidates have already worked with the regulations throughout preparation.

NFPA 58 should be reviewed when studying LP-gas concepts. Learn the organization of the standard and become familiar with sections involving containers, piping, system equipment, installation, protection, and safety. Candidates should be able to distinguish when a question is better addressed by the International Fuel Gas Code and when an LP-gas-specific reference may be more useful.

Open-book study should be active. When completing a practice question, identify the topic before opening a book. Choose the most relevant reference and locate the supporting information. If the answer is incorrect, read the surrounding code section to understand the underlying requirement rather than simply memorizing the correct choice.

Timed practice can also help candidates improve pacing. Work through groups of questions while monitoring how long it takes to answer straightforward technical questions, locate code provisions, and complete pipe-sizing problems. This can help identify reference sections that require greater familiarity.

The goal is to combine technical understanding with efficient use of the books. Candidates who know the subject and know where supporting information is located can approach open-book questions more systematically.

This package is designed for candidates pursuing the Virginia Landscape Service Contracting specialty (LSC) who want the listed references together in one organized exam-preparation package.

Landscape service contracting involves much more than planting and routine landscape maintenance. Virginia's LSC specialty includes alteration or improvement of land through activities such as excavation, clearing, grading, construction of retaining walls for landscaping purposes, placement of landscaping timbers, and removal of stumps and roots below grade.

The technical knowledge associated with this work can involve estimating, earthmoving, soil conditions, excavation equipment, compaction, drainage, site preparation, retaining-wall construction, and construction safety. Candidates should be prepared to understand how these subjects work together on a landscape construction project.

The Virginia Landscaping Service Contracting Exam Complete Book Package includes references covering those major areas. OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 supports construction-safety preparation. Pipe and Excavation Contracting addresses excavation and underground construction concepts. Construction Planning, Equipment, and Methods provides information about construction operations and equipment. The Excavation and Grading Handbook focuses on earthmoving and grading, while Soils and Foundations supports soil-related preparation.

Landscape Construction provides trade-focused information for landscape projects, and Fences & Retaining Walls provides additional material involving barriers and retaining-wall construction.

Because the Virginia Landscape Service Contracting examination is open book, candidates should work with their references throughout preparation. The objective is not merely to own the books, but to understand which reference is most likely to address a particular question and how to locate that information efficiently.

What You Get

  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
  • Pipe and Excavation Contracting
  • Construction Planning, Equipment, and Methods, 10th Edition
  • Excavation and Grading Handbook, Nick Capachi, 2006

  • Landscape Construction, 2011
  • Fences & Retaining Walls (USED)

Exam Details

The Virginia Landscape Service Contracting examination is the technical specialty examination associated with the LSC designation. Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation through the Board for Contractors.

  • Specialty: Landscape Service Contracting
  • Specialty Abbreviation: LSC
  • Number of Questions: 50
  • Time Allowed: 120 minutes
  • Passing Score: 70%, or 35 correct answers
  • Testing Provider: PSI

Major areas associated with Landscape Service Contracting preparation include planning and estimating, excavation, grading, compaction, drainage, soils, vegetation removal, retaining walls, and construction safety.

These subjects are closely related. An excavation question may also involve soil conditions or equipment selection. A grading problem may require an understanding of drainage. Retaining-wall work can involve excavation, soil behavior, drainage, construction materials, and safe work practices.

Candidates should therefore prepare by understanding complete construction processes rather than memorizing isolated terms. Knowing why a particular excavation, compaction, grading, or drainage method is used can help when interpreting technical examination questions.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Landscape Service Contracting examination is an open book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing allowable reference materials into the examination and following the applicable PSI rules governing those materials.

Open-book testing makes reference navigation an important preparation skill. With 50 questions and 120 minutes available, candidates have an average of approximately two minutes and twenty-four seconds per question. Spending too much time searching through an unrelated reference can make time management more difficult.

Before opening a book, identify the subject. A construction-safety question should direct attention toward OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926. An excavation or underground construction question may point toward Pipe and Excavation Contracting. Questions involving earthmoving, cuts, fills, or grading may be better addressed through the Excavation and Grading Handbook.

Soil-related questions may require Soils and Foundations. Construction-equipment and planning questions may direct candidates toward Construction Planning, Equipment, and Methods. Landscape-specific construction subjects can be reviewed in Landscape Construction, while retaining-wall or fence subjects may require Fences & Retaining Walls.

Practice this process regularly. Review the table of contents and index in each reference, identify major chapters, and become familiar with the terminology each book uses. That familiarity can help candidates determine where to begin looking when a question requires a reference lookup.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing involves the contracting business, its license class, and the classifications or specialty designations under which it operates. The technical LSC examination is one component of that process.

  1. Determine the appropriate Virginia contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select Landscape Service Contracting. The specialty abbreviation is LSC.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. The contracting business must designate a Qualified Individual for the requested specialty.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirement. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the experience requirement associated with the requested license class.
  5. Complete required pre-license education. New Virginia contractor applicants must satisfy the state's applicable pre-license education requirement.
  6. Receive pre-approval for the technical examination. Landscape Service Contracting is among the Virginia specialties requiring pre-approval and successful completion of a technical exam.
  7. Prepare for the LSC specialty examination. Study planning, estimating, excavation, grading, compaction, drainage, soils, retaining walls, vegetation removal, and safety.
  8. Complete additional requirements for the selected license class. Additional business examination and licensing requirements may apply according to the class being pursued.
  9. Submit the contractor license application. Complete the applicable Virginia Board for Contractors application and provide the required supporting documentation.

Passing the LSC technical examination does not by itself issue a Virginia contractor license. The business must satisfy the complete requirements associated with its selected license class and specialty.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Landscape Service Contracting as work that alters or improves a land area, when that work is not related to another classification or specialty, by means of excavation, clearing, grading, construction of retaining walls for landscaping purposes, or placement of landscaping timbers.

The specialty may also remove stumps and roots below grade. Certain broader Virginia contractor classifications also provide for the landscape service contracting function within their authorized scopes.

The LSC specialty should not be confused with Landscape Irrigation Contracting. Landscape irrigation is a separate Virginia contractor specialty addressing irrigation sprinkler and outdoor sprinkler systems.

The contractor business must identify a Qualified Individual for the LSC specialty and meet the applicable licensing requirements. The Qualified Individual must meet the experience requirements associated with the requested license class and successfully satisfy the technical examination requirement.

Virginia also requires pre-license education for new Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses. This business-focused requirement is separate from preparation for the Landscape Service Contracting technical examination.

Reference Books

  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    This federal construction-safety reference supports preparation involving excavation safety, protective equipment, equipment operation, trenches, ladders, electrical hazards, material handling, and other construction-site safety requirements.
  • Pipe and Excavation Contracting
    This trade reference addresses excavation and underground construction concepts. It supports preparation involving trenching, excavation operations, grading, equipment, underground work, and related field practices.
  • Construction Planning, Equipment, and Methods, 10th Edition
    This reference covers construction planning, equipment selection, productivity, earthmoving operations, construction methods, and related project considerations. It can help candidates connect equipment capabilities with excavation, grading, and site-work operations.
  • Excavation and Grading Handbook, Nick Capachi, 2006
    This practical reference focuses on excavation, grading, earthmoving, cut-and-fill work, compaction, site preparation, and related construction procedures.
  • Soils and Foundations, Cheng Liu and Jack B. Evett, 2008, 7th Edition
    This reference supports preparation involving soil characteristics, soil behavior, compaction, foundations, bearing conditions, and other soil-related concepts that can affect landscape construction and earthwork.
  • Landscape Construction, 2011
    This landscape-focused construction reference supports preparation involving site work, landscape construction methods, drainage, hardscape-related work, project organization, and other practical landscape construction subjects.

    This reference provides practical information involving fence and retaining-wall construction, including layout, materials, construction concepts, and related installation considerations. The copy included in this package is identified as used.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong LSC preparation plan should begin with planning and estimating. Candidates should be comfortable reading dimensions, calculating quantities, considering job conditions, and connecting project requirements with materials, equipment, and labor needs.

Excavation should receive focused study because landscape construction frequently begins with site preparation and earthmoving. Review excavation terminology, methods, equipment, trenching concepts, cut-and-fill work, and safe excavation practices.

Grading is closely connected to drainage and site performance. Candidates should understand how grades influence water movement and how earthwork is used to create the required finished elevations.

Compaction should be studied together with soil conditions. Different soils behave differently when placed, disturbed, or compacted. Use Soils and Foundations together with the excavation references to strengthen understanding of soil behavior and site preparation.

Drainage is an important landscape construction subject because poor water management can affect soils, retaining walls, landscaped areas, and surrounding improvements. Review grading concepts and landscape construction principles that influence drainage.

Vegetation removal can involve clearing, stump removal, roots, excavation equipment, and site-safety considerations. Candidates should understand that the Virginia LSC specialty specifically includes the ability to remove stumps and roots below grade.

For retaining walls, use the landscape, soil, excavation, and retaining-wall references together. Retaining-wall construction can involve excavation, foundations, backfill, drainage, soil pressure, materials, and site conditions.

Safety should be incorporated throughout preparation. Landscape service contracting can involve heavy equipment, excavation, trenches, hand and power tools, material handling, and active construction areas. OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 provides the primary construction-safety reference included in the package.

When studying, avoid reading every reference from beginning to end without a plan. Organize preparation around the exam subjects. Choose a topic such as grading, identify the reference most likely to contain that information, and practice locating it through the index and table of contents.

Repeated reference use helps create a mental map of the books. Over time, candidates can learn that soil properties belong in one reference, excavation practices in another, and landscape-specific construction material in another.

When a practice question is missed, return to the relevant reference and determine why. The error may come from misunderstanding a soil concept, selecting the wrong construction method, making an estimating mistake, or searching the wrong book. Correcting the underlying problem can strengthen future preparation.

Landscape construction combines planning, estimating, excavation, soils, equipment, grading, drainage, retaining walls, vegetation removal, and construction safety, making a structured preparation routine especially valuable.

The Complete Book Package provides the listed references in one collection so candidates can build familiarity with each source while studying the trade. Instead of relying solely on memorization, candidates can learn how the books relate to specific technical subjects.

1 Exam Prep emphasizes organized study guidance, trade-focused review, practice-oriented preparation, reference navigation when applicable, and confidence-building study structure.

For an open-book examination, reference familiarity is a practical advantage. Candidates who recognize which book addresses a subject can begin their lookup more efficiently and spend more time understanding the actual technical requirement.

The goal is to build stronger landscape construction knowledge and more effective reference-navigation habits. Consistent practice with excavation, grading, soils, equipment, retaining walls, landscape construction, and OSHA material can help candidates develop a more systematic approach to exam preparation.

Exam Details

The Virginia Marine Facility Contracting examination is the technical specialty examination associated with the MCC designation. The Virginia Board for Contractors regulates contractor licensing, and PSI administers the specialty examination program.

  • Specialty: Marine Facility Contracting
  • Specialty Abbreviation: MCC
  • Number of Questions: 50
  • Time Allowed: 120 minutes
  • Passing Score: 70%, or 35 correct answers
  • Testing Provider: PSI

The examination requires familiarity with the technical principles associated with marine construction. Candidates should prepare for subjects involving construction methods, concrete, reinforcement, equipment, and safety. These subjects often overlap in actual construction work, so preparation should focus on understanding complete construction processes rather than isolated terms.

For example, a reinforced concrete structure may involve concrete mixture design, reinforcing-bar placement, structural requirements, equipment selection, material handling, sequencing, and jobsite safety. Understanding how these topics connect can make technical questions easier to analyze.

With 50 questions and 120 minutes available, candidates have an average of approximately two minutes and twenty-four seconds per question. Strong reference-navigation habits can help candidates make better use of that time when a technical provision needs to be located.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Marine Facility Contracting examination is an open book test. Candidates may bring allowable reference materials into the examination, subject to the current PSI rules governing those materials.

Allowable references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the exam. Permanent tabs are permitted, while temporary or removable tabs are not allowed. Candidates should become familiar with the examination reference rules before test day and prepare their books accordingly.

The open-book format should not be treated as a substitute for study. Searching through several unfamiliar books for every question can use too much time. A stronger strategy is to identify the technical subject first and then choose the reference most likely to contain the relevant information.

A construction-safety question may direct attention toward 29 CFR Part 1926. A question involving equipment or project operations may point toward Construction Planning, Equipment, and Methods. Reinforcing-bar questions can require Placing Reinforcing Bars, while concrete-material questions may be supported by Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures.

When a question involves structural concrete requirements, candidates should be prepared to navigate ACI 318-14. Learning where major subjects appear in the code can make the book much easier to use during an exam.

Reference navigation should be practiced throughout the course. Start with a topic, identify the correct book, use the table of contents or index, locate the section, and read enough surrounding material to understand the requirement in context.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing involves both the contracting business and the Qualified Individual associated with the requested specialty. Passing the MCC technical exam is one component of the overall licensing process.

  1. Determine the appropriate contractor license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select Marine Facility Contracting. MCC is the specialty designation for qualifying marine facility construction work.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. The contracting business must designate a Qualified Individual for the requested specialty.
  4. Meet applicable experience requirements. The Qualified Individual must satisfy the experience requirements associated with the license class being pursued.
  5. Complete required pre-license education. New Virginia Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor license applicants must complete eight hours of approved pre-license education.
  6. Receive eligibility approval for the MCC examination. Marine Facility Contracting requires successful completion of the applicable technical specialty exam.
  7. Prepare for the technical examination. Study construction safety, equipment, methods, reinforcement, concrete materials, and structural concrete requirements.
  8. Complete additional requirements associated with the selected license class. Business examination and other licensing requirements may apply depending on the class being pursued.
  9. Submit the contractor license application. Complete the Virginia Board for Contractors application process and provide the required supporting documentation.

Successful completion of the technical examination does not by itself issue a contractor license. The business must satisfy the complete requirements applicable to its selected license class and Marine Facility Contracting specialty.

State Requirements

Virginia defines Marine Facility Contracting as the service that provides for the construction, repair, improvement, or removal of a structure whose purpose is to provide access to, impede, or alter a body of surface water.

The Commercial Building Contractor and Highway/Heavy classifications also provide for the marine facility function within their authorized scopes.

The MCC specialty does not provide for construction of accessory structures or for electrical, HVAC, or plumbing functions. Work falling outside the defined MCC scope requires the appropriate authorization.

The Virginia contractor license itself consists of two major components: the license class and the classification or specialty. The license class addresses the monetary level of work the business may perform, while the classification or specialty determines the type of work authorized.

The contractor business must also designate a Qualified Individual who meets the applicable requirements for the requested specialty. Candidates preparing for the MCC exam should therefore understand that technical exam completion is part of a broader licensing process.

The Virginia Masonry Contractor exam covers much more than basic brick and block installation. Candidates are expected to understand topics involving estimating and plan reading, unit masonry, mortar and grout, accessories and specialties, stone, masonry tools, restoration and cleaning, reinforced masonry, and construction safety. Kicklighter, 10th Edition, the Indiana Limestone Handbook, 22nd Edition, 2007, and Repointing Mortar Joints in Historic Masonry Buildings by Robert C. Mack and John P. Speweik, October 1998.

These references address different parts of the knowledge expected from a masonry contractor. Studying them alongside organized exam-preparation material can help candidates understand which resource to use for a particular type of question and develop a more efficient approach to open-book testing.

Exam Details

The Virginia Masonry Contracting specialty is identified as BRK by the Virginia Board for Contractors. Masonry Contracting covers work involving brick, concrete block, stone, marble, slate, and other masonry products, as well as related masonry activities within the specialty's defined scope.

The Virginia Masonry Contracting examination contains 60 questions. Candidates are allowed 150 minutes to complete the exam. A passing score of 70 percent requires 42 correct answers.

The official exam content is divided into multiple knowledge areas:

  • Estimating and Plan Reading: 5 questions
  • Unit Masonry: 12 questions
  • Mortar and Grout: 11 questions
  • Accessories and Specialties: 10 questions
  • Stone: 3 questions
  • Tools: 4 questions
  • Restoration and Cleaning: 4 questions
  • Reinforced Masonry: 6 questions
  • Safety: 5 questions

This distribution shows why a balanced study plan is important. Unit masonry, mortar and grout, and accessories and specialties account for a substantial portion of the examination, but candidates should not overlook smaller areas such as stone, tools, restoration, reinforced masonry, estimating, or safety.

The Masonry specialty requires the applicable Qualified Individual to meet Virginia qualification requirements and successfully complete the required technical examination. BRK is among the contractor specialties for which examination approval is required.

Open Book Test

The Virginia Masonry Contractor examination is open book. Candidates must bring their own permitted references because examination books are not supplied at the testing site.

Open-book testing changes the way candidates should prepare. The objective is not simply to memorize every detail in every book. Candidates should build enough trade knowledge to recognize the subject of a question and enough familiarity with the references to know where the supporting information is likely to be located.

Reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed when prepared according to PSI examination rules. Permanent tabs may be used, while removable tabs are prohibited. Candidates should follow the current testing rules when preparing any books that will be taken into the examination.

With 60 questions and 150 minutes, candidates have an average of approximately two and a half minutes per question. Some questions may be answered quickly through trade knowledge, while others may require finding information in a code, safety standard, trade reference, stone handbook, or restoration publication. Practicing reference navigation before test day helps reduce time spent searching.

A useful open-book strategy is to identify the subject first. A construction-safety question should direct attention toward 29 CFR Part 1926. A building-code requirement may point toward the 2021 International Building Code. Questions involving masonry installation and materials may require Modern Masonry. Limestone questions may involve the Indiana Limestone Handbook, while historic mortar repair may require the repointing publication.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation through the Board for Contractors. Contractor licenses are issued to businesses and consist of a license class together with one or more classifications or specialty designations.

  1. Determine the appropriate contractor license class. Virginia contractor licenses are issued as Class A, Class B, or Class C.
  2. Select the Masonry Contracting specialty. Masonry Contracting is identified by the BRK specialty designation.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. A contractor business must identify a Qualified Individual for each classification or specialty requested.
  4. Meet the applicable experience requirement. The required amount of experience depends on the contractor license class being pursued.
  5. Complete required pre-license education. New Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor applicants must satisfy Virginia's eight-hour pre-license education requirement.
  6. Obtain approval for the technical examination. The Masonry specialty requires pre-approval for the Qualified Individual examination.
  7. Prepare for and successfully complete the Masonry examination. Study the required trade subjects and become familiar with the approved exam references.
  8. Complete the contractor license application requirements. The business must meet the applicable requirements for its selected license class, Qualified Individual, Responsible Management, examinations, documentation, and application.

Virginia requires successful completion of applicable examinations before contractor licensure is issued. Candidates pursuing the Masonry specialty should therefore plan their exam preparation as one part of the broader contractor licensing process.

State Requirements

The Virginia Board for Contractors regulates contractor businesses performing construction, removal, repair, and improvement work on property owned by others. Each contractor license includes a class and one or more classifications or specialties. The license class governs the level of contracting activity, while the classification or specialty determines the type of work the contractor may perform.

Each contractor business must name a Qualified Individual for the classification or specialty requested. For current Virginia applications, the Qualified Individual must be a member of Responsible Management or a qualifying full-time employee of the business.

The experience requirement depends on the license class. A Qualified Individual for a Class C business must have at least one year of experience in the applicable classification or specialty. Class B requires at least three years of experience, while Class A requires at least five years.

Masonry, identified as BRK, is one of the specialties for which applicants are required to be pre-approved and successfully complete an examination. An Experience Verification Form is required for Qualified Individuals seeking a designation that requires pre-approval for an examination.

Virginia also requires eight hours of approved pre-license education for new Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses. This education is a separate business and regulatory requirement and is not the same as the Masonry technical examination.

    The 2021 International Building Code contains building requirements relevant to regulated construction. Candidates should practice navigating the code by chapter, section, definition, table, index entry, and cross-reference so that masonry-related requirements can be located efficiently.

    This trade reference covers masonry materials and methods involving brick, block, stone, mortar, grout, tools, layout, construction procedures, wall systems, and related masonry knowledge. It provides an important foundation for many of the practical trade subjects represented on the exam.

    This specialized stone reference addresses Indiana limestone and provides information related to stone characteristics, detailing, fabrication, anchorage, joints, handling, and installation. Candidates should know how the handbook is organized before working through stone-related exam questions.
  • Repointing Mortar Joints in Historic Masonry Buildings, Robert C. Mack and John P. Speweik, October 1998
    This masonry-preservation reference addresses the evaluation and repair of deteriorated mortar joints in historic masonry. It includes information involving mortar selection, joint preparation, removal of deteriorated mortar, repointing procedures, tooling, curing, and cleaning.

A stronger approach is to understand the major trade concepts and know which reference is most likely to contain the information needed for a particular question.

Permitted examination references may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the test. Permanent tabs may be used in accordance with PSI testing requirements. Removable tabs are not permitted, and candidates may not write in their reference materials during the examination.

Reference-navigation practice should therefore be part of the study process. Students should learn how each book is organized and practice locating information by chapter, section, table, index term, and subject. Repeated use helps build familiarity that can reduce unnecessary searching during the examination.

For example, construction-safety questions may direct the candidate toward 29 CFR Part 1926. Building-code questions may involve the 2021 International Building Code. General masonry construction questions may require Modern Masonry, while stone and historic restoration questions may direct candidates toward the Indiana Limestone Handbook or the publication on repointing historic masonry.

Licensing Steps

Virginia contractor licensing is administered by the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation through the Board for Contractors. Contractor licenses are issued to businesses and include a license class together with one or more classifications or specialty designations.

  1. Select the appropriate license class. Virginia issues Class A, Class B, and Class C contractor licenses.
  2. Select the Masonry Contracting specialty. Masonry Contracting is identified as BRK.
  3. Identify the Qualified Individual. The contractor business must identify a Qualified Individual for each classification or specialty requested.
  4. Meet the required experience level. The amount of experience required for the Qualified Individual depends on the contractor license class being pursued.
  5. Complete the required pre-license education. New Virginia contractor license applicants must satisfy the current Board-approved pre-license education requirement.
  6. Obtain approval for the BRK examination. Masonry is one of the specialties requiring pre-approval before the applicable technical examination.
  7. Prepare for and complete the required examination. Candidates should study the examination content areas and become familiar with the technical references permitted for testing.
  8. Complete the contractor license application requirements. The business must satisfy the applicable requirements for its license class, Responsible Management, Qualified Individual, examination, documentation, and application.

Virginia requires the applicable examination to be successfully completed before the contractor license application is submitted. Candidates should treat BRK exam preparation as one part of the larger contractor licensing process.

State Requirements

The Virginia Board for Contractors regulates contractor businesses. A Virginia contractor license consists of a license class and one or more classifications or specialties. The class determines the level of contracting activity authorized, while the classification or specialty determines the type of work the business may perform.

A business seeking the Masonry specialty must designate a Qualified Individual. The Qualified Individual must be a member of Responsible Management or a qualifying full-time employee of the business working at least 30 hours per week.

The minimum experience requirement for a Qualified Individual depends on the license class. Virginia requires at least one year of experience for Class C, three years for Class B, and five years for Class A in the applicable classification or specialty.

BRK Masonry is among the classifications and specialties for which the Qualified Individual must be pre-approved and pass the applicable examination. An Experience Verification Form is required for Qualified Individuals requesting a designation that requires examination pre-approval.

Virginia also requires Board-approved pre-license education for new contractor licenses. This education focuses on business principles, regulations, and requirements of contractor licensure. It is separate from the BRK Masonry technical examination and from trade-focused Masonry exam preparation.

It provides a useful foundation for many of the trade subjects represented on the BRK examination.
  • Indiana Limestone Handbook, 22nd Edition, 2007
    This specialized reference addresses Indiana limestone and includes information associated with natural stone characteristics, detailing, fabrication, joints, anchorage, handling, and installation. Candidates should become familiar with its organization when preparing for stone-related questions.
  • Repointing Mortar Joints in Historic Masonry Buildings, Robert C. Mack and John P. Speweik, October 1998
    This preservation publication addresses repair of deteriorated mortar joints in historic masonry. Subjects include mortar selection, removal of deteriorated mortar, joint preparation, repointing procedures, tooling, curing, and cleaning.

A productive study plan should connect each examination category with the reference material and trade knowledge most likely to support it. Instead of reading every book from beginning to end without a plan, candidates can divide preparation into focused subject areas and practice locating information as they study.

For estimating and plan reading, review the types of dimensions, quantities, and construction information used to evaluate masonry work. Candidates should be comfortable interpreting information and determining what is needed to complete masonry-related calculations or decisions.

Accessories and specialties account for 10 questions. Candidates should understand components used with masonry construction and how those components interact with masonry assemblies. Reinforced masonry should also receive focused review because it represents six additional questions.

Construction-safety preparation should include direct practice with 29 CFR Part 1926. Rather than attempting to memorize the entire federal safety standard, become familiar with its structure and learn how to locate information about major construction hazards.

Code preparation should involve regular use of the 2021 International Building Code. Practice moving from an index term to a chapter, section, table, or related provision. Learning how the code is organized can make code-based questions easier to manage during an open-book examination.

Stone preparation should incorporate the Indiana Limestone Handbook, while restoration and cleaning preparation should include Repointing Mortar Joints in Historic Masonry Buildings. Candidates should know which specialized reference applies to a question before spending time searching.
